title_en: GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
title_fa: GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
excerpt_en: That would be a much smaller port time than GTA 5.
excerpt_fa: That would be a much smaller port time than GTA 5.
content_en:
GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
PC players might be able to dive into Jason and Lucia's story by the end of March.
PC players may not have to wait too much longer to jump into Grand Theft Auto 6. According to GamesBeat's sources, Rockstar Games' upcoming blockbuster will hit PC in the first quarter of 2027, just a few months after its debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19.
That's a much shorter window than Grand Theft Auto 5's initial release on consoles and its arrival on PC. The previous game in the series made its debut on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on September 17, 2013. It didn't come to PC until April 2015.
Most other developers and publishers have given GTA 6 a wide berth this fall, as it's all but guaranteed to be a massive hit that captures the attention of many players. It could well be the case that games that were supposed to arrive early next year end up being delayed to avoid competing with the PC port as well. The release slate for the first quarter of 2027 currently includes Stranger Than Heaven, Metroid Ravenous, Until Dawn 2, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, God of War Laufey and Fable.
It's not clear when Rockstar will add the inevitable online mode (about which it's been tight-lipped) to GTA 6 either. However, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has claimed that'll happen next year. For what it's worth, the hugely popular GTA 5 roleplaying mods are PC-only. Rockstar recently added a GTA 5 roleplaying option to its PC launcher, three years after it acquired the team behind roleplaying server company FiveM. Connecting the dots here, the company may be waiting until it releases the PC version of GTA 6 before it switches on multiplayer.

title_en: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
title_fa: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
excerpt_en: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
excerpt_fa: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
content_en:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security, says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.
Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.
Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.
Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.
That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.
When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.
“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”
Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.
“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.
In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.
To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.
What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.
“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.
The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. Developers rank fourth, she said.
Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.

When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.

title_en: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
title_fa: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
excerpt_en: Diesel is expensive and polluting, and LNK Energies says it has come up with a way to replace it with hydrogen, all while undercutting diesel on cost.
excerpt_fa: Diesel is expensive and polluting, and LNK Energies says it has come up with a way to replace it with hydrogen, all while undercutting diesel on cost.
content_en:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout.
For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.
LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)
Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly.
LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.
“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”
Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch.
In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.
The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”
Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck.
The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.
LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.

title_en: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
title_fa: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
excerpt_en: Google is making it easier to build and use personal Android apps created with AI, without having to make them available to everyone on the Play Store.
excerpt_fa: Google is making it easier to build and use personal Android apps created with AI, without having to make them available to everyone on the Play Store.
content_en:
Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private.
These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator.
The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android.
Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use.
These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android.
Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up.
“That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.”
In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store.
And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews.
Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players.
Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates.
Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations.
The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience.

title_en: Google will let you distribute vibe-coded Android apps with just a Google account
title_fa: Google will let you distribute vibe-coded Android apps with just a Google account
excerpt_en: The company is revamping the Play Store for the AI era with changes to publishing, recommendations and more.
excerpt_fa: The company is revamping the Play Store for the AI era with changes to publishing, recommendations and more.
content_en:
Google will let you distribute vibe-coded Android apps with just a Google account
The company is revamping the Play Store for the AI era with changes to publishing, recommendations and more.
As part of a collection of updates to the Play Store, Google has announced that it will allow anyone who vibe codes an Android app to distribute it through the Play Store with just a Google account. The company's app store has changed a lot in the last few years, both in the wake of Google's efforts to inject AI into everything and legal pressure the company has faced to open the Play Store to competitors. But this change could prove to be one of the biggest.
Users have been able to sideload APKs of Android apps to their phones or tablets for a while, with Google making the process more complex in the last year. This new publishing process will make things easier. Rolling out to users in the US and other select markets who are 18 years and up, Google will let you upload a vibe-coded Android app from Google AI Studio without a paid developer account. For those who aren't familiar, Google's AI Studio is capable of generating apps with just a written prompt to Gemini, and you can adjust your results with more prompts or directly editing the generated code yourself.
Your app will only be available on your own devices to start (including tablets and computers with access to the Play Store) in a new "personal library" section, but Google eventually plans to let you securely share your vibe-coded apps with friends and family, too. When you want to distribute your apps to a global audience, the company says it will also be possible to "graduate" to a professional developer account and submit your apps to the Play Store's normal safety reviews.
Alongside this major change to app publishing, Google is also making tweaks to app discovery and its ever-growing list of gaming-focused features. The company already introduced its biggest change, Ask Play, at I/O 2026, but now it's also bringing similar app discovery features to Gemini by allowing the AI assistant to surface direct links to Play Store apps in chats. Google will also feature more apps through its sports topic pages that appear in the Play Store during live matches. They'll now expand to cover soccer games from Premier League, Major League Soccer and more. In cars with Google built-in and Android XR, the company is also updating the Play Store's layout to better fit the size of your physical or virtual screen.
If you're specifically interested in finding games, the new Game Finder feature can recommend things to play that fit your unique taste. Google says it's able to offer these recommendations based on your Gamer DNA, a new taste profile that you can finetune with your preferences and favorite genres. In a roundtable with press, Google suggested it hopes to make the filters and genre tags increasingly granular, opening up the possibility of drilling down into, say, games that specifically offer controller support, for example. You can also find new things to play via the new game playlists feature, which lets you recommend a collection of mobile games for other people to try.
The company is updating the overall experience of playing games on Android, too. Its Sidekick overlay has a new feature that allows it to record 30-second clips of gameplay, and developers are receiving a collection of new tools they can use to increase engagement. These include Sprints, Community Posts and an expansion of the Quests feature.
Sprints are 48-hour in-game challenges that match you with players of a similar skill level to compete for the highest score. Quests, which allowed developers to reward players with Play Points, now also lets them provide in-game rewards. Finally, Community Posts adds a Q&A section to store pages so players can ask and answer questions about games in the Play Store.
The helpfulness of these new features depends a lot on your faith in AI's ability to build apps and offer recommendations. But they're a sign that Google is trying to stay competitive with third-party app stores now that they can be installed through the Play Store.

title_en: Netflix will broadcast the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra
title_fa: Netflix will broadcast the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra
excerpt_en: Get those VPNs ready.
excerpt_fa: Get those VPNs ready.
content_en:
Netflix will broadcast the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra
This includes all 104 matches, with one free event per day.
Netflix will stream the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra, which is the very first time the platform will broadcast the traditional World Cup. This isn't just Netflix getting its mitts on a couple of matches. The streamer will show all 104 matches throughout the event, but again, only to viewers in Spain and Andorra.
The company has also vowed to make one match each day available for free via unnamed national broadcasters, to comply with local laws. This includes every game that Spain participates in, as they are a host country, in addition to both semi-finals and the final. The remaining matches will require a subscription.
Netflix has secured exclusive broadcasting rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra, giving the streaming giant all 104 matches of the tournament.https://t.co/CVNYrx5IoV
— Variety (@Variety) October 13, 2026
In addition to full coverage of the tournament itself, Netflix will air pre-game, halftime and post-game shows. There will also be a daily round-up show on match days. This sounds like a nice little package for fans, some of whom may or may not be using a VPN.
This isn't the only move Netflix has made to cozy up to FIFA. The platform has secured the US broadcast rights to the 2027 and 2031 Women's World Cup tournaments.

title_en: Here's why your phone's proximity sensors are so important
title_fa: Here's why your phone's proximity sensors are so important
excerpt_en: Your phone would lose a long list of features and basic functions if it didn't have proximity sensors.
excerpt_fa: Your phone would lose a long list of features and basic functions if it didn't have proximity sensors.
content_en:
Here's why your phone's proximity sensors are so important
They do way more than you might think.
Any recent smartphone, be it an Android device or an iPhone, is chock-full of sensors. It wasn't always this way, but after the original 2007 iPhone, many sensor-reliant features quickly became standard. And of course, phone makers are constantly trying to one-up each other, sometimes in ridiculous ways. For a few years, some Google Pixel phones offered external temperature readers — no matter that even if the technology were bulletproof, a phone would still be an unreliable way to check for fever, never mind whether your chicken is done.
Particularly important are proximity sensors. These are actually a category rather than a specific kind of sensor, but they're so critical that the phone you're using has several of them. Arguably, smartphones would be impossible without them.
Here we're going to cover what constitutes a proximity sensor and how your phone uses this data. Some good news is that the data is rarely of interest to anyone but yourself. With, perhaps, a couple of major exceptions.
The main proximity sensors in your smartphone
The most basic proximity sensor in your phone is the one used to shut off the screen whenever you raise it to your ear. This relies on infrared and/or capacitive technology. It not only prevents accidental touch commands, but also extends battery life, since the display will always be one of your phone's most power-hungry components. It's pointless for it to outshine the sun while you're on a 40-minute tech support call.
Some phones rely on advanced infrared sensors to detect when you are nearby. The best example of this is Apple's Face ID, which projects a series of dots to create a facial depth map and compares that against one you saved during calibration. The main purpose of this is replacing passcode and password logins. In some cases, however, facial recognition is "attention-aware" — meaning that whether or not you're looking will determine things like screen brightness, alert volume or whether sensitive content is shown. Given the potential for abuse, companies go to extreme lengths to prevent facial recognition data from leaving your phone, including heavily encrypted authentication chips.
Another sensor connected to valuable info is your phone's NFC (near-field communication) chip. This detects a similarly equipped device and transmits data over an extremely short distance, generally just an inch or two. But because this enables things like retail payments, digital keys, device pairing and direct file transfers, it's crucial that only vetted apps have access.
The sensors you might have missed
Most touchscreens can be considered proximity sensors, actually. While pressure-sensitive screens exist, anyone who's used them can vouch for how cumbersome they are. Capacitive screens instead react to the electricity in your body, so even the slightest gesture will register. title_en: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s
title_fa: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s
excerpt_en: Satlyt wants to be the Android of orbital computing, offering open software that works on many companies' satellites, versus SpaceX's closed, all-in-one iPhone-style approach.
excerpt_fa: Satlyt wants to be the Android of orbital computing, offering open software that works on many companies' satellites, versus SpaceX's closed, all-in-one iPhone-style approach.
content_en:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.
The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.
“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.
So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.
The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.
Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.
Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.
Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.
A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.
Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.
The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.
Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.
One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”
Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.
“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here.

title_en: Apple HomePod mini 2 vs. Apple HomePod mini: What do you get for the $50 increase?
title_fa: Apple HomePod mini 2 vs. Apple HomePod mini: What do you get for the $50 increase?
excerpt_en: Are Siri AI, a new chip and Sound Glow worth the higher price?
excerpt_fa: Are Siri AI, a new chip and Sound Glow worth the higher price?
content_en:
Apple HomePod mini 2 vs. Apple HomePod mini: What do you get for the $50 increase?
The main differences are Siri AI, a new chip and Sound Glow.
At its 'Welcome Home" event today, Apple unveiled the HomePod mini 2 — a long-awaited update to its smart speaker, which hadn't been updated since its launch in 2020. On the outside, it looks pretty much the same, but the new model comes with some cool surprises on the inside. You get Siri AI and a few other features for those living in the Apple ecosystem — but all of this comes at a price. The HomePod mini 2 costs $149, which is $50 more than the original's launch price six years ago. Are the updates are really worth the extra cost? Should owners of the first HomePod mini upgrade? Let's break down the differences to find out.
What's new on the HomePod mini 2
The main difference between the HomePod mini 2 and the original, at least from a hardware standpoint, is its processor. The new model's Apple S10 chip replaces the S5 from 2019, which was the same chip found in the Apple Watch Series 5. The S10 is more powerful and enables Siri AI for the first time on a HomePod — though the smarter assistant won't be available at launch. But how it works on the new HomePod mini 2 also depends on which phone you have.
By default, Siri AI on the HomePod can conduct natural conversations and answer general knowledge questions more accurately than its predecessor. Of course, it can also play songs and podcasts just like before, but now you can do so with more natural voice commands. For example, you could ask it to play only the surprise songs from Taylor Swift's The Eras Tour — something the old Siri can't do. But here's the catch: to get personalized context, the HomePod mini 2 needs to be paired with an iPhone or iPad with Apple Intelligence. With a compatible device, you'll get even more features with Siri AI, such as responses based on your emails, messages and calendar.
Another subtle but cool new feature is Sound Glow. Just like before, the HomePod mini 2 has a touch-sensitive surface for media controls with glowing lights. But now, the lights will sync with the music playing and react to the bass and treble, using colors from the album artwork. Sound Glow is also another feature that requires pairing the HomePod mini 2 with an iPhone or iPad running Apple Intelligence.
Apple didn't mention any new drivers or significant acoustic improvements, but it claims that the S10 chip enhances what it calls computational audio. For instance, you can now set up a surround sound system using four HomePod mini 2 units or a pair of HomePod mini 2 and another couple of HomePod 2 (the bigger one), all connected to the new Apple TV.
Is it really worth paying extra for the HomePod mini 2?
Whether the HomePod mini 2 is worth the price really depends on how you use your speakers. If you already have a bunch of HomePod minis in your home, don't rush to upgrade them all at once — especially since Siri AI won't be available until later this year. Enhancements like Sound Glow are cool, but they don't really add much to the experience you already have with the original HomePod mini, especially since there aren't real upgrades to the sound system. Of course, if you're already in the market for a new HomePod mini anyway, you should definitely get the new model.
The upgrade starts to make more sense for those planning to build their own home theater system with Apple TV and HomePods. The ability to pair two sets together to create surround sound setups seems promising, especially since the speakers detect their position in the room to automatically calibrate the audio. Also, Mac users will finally be able to use a pair of HomePod mini 2 as their default speakers, with low latency and even the ability to use the built-in microphones for FaceTime calls. If all these features strike you as appealing, the extra cost might end up being worth it.

title_en: Is AppleCare actually worth it for the Apple Watch SE?
title_fa: Is AppleCare actually worth it for the Apple Watch SE?
excerpt_en: AppleCare+ makes Apple Watch repairs or replacements easier, but even at a low cost, it might not be a good value.
excerpt_fa: AppleCare+ makes Apple Watch repairs or replacements easier, but even at a low cost, it might not be a good value.
content_en:
Is AppleCare actually worth it for the Apple Watch SE?
The affordable coverage is worth a look, but it isn’t for everyone.
AppleCare+ is relatively inexpensive for the Apple Watch SE 3: $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year for the Theft and Loss plan. That's much less than the average streaming subscription. The plan includes unlimited accidental damage incidents, along with battery service and up to two theft or loss claims per year.
But AppleCare+ is not a complete coverage option because there are stipulations and additional costs. Whether it's worth the cost depends on your typical day-to-day. There's a big difference between wearing an Apple Watch while working from home and welding for a living. Service for accidental damage to the SE 3 will still cost you $69 per incident, and a theft or loss replacement comes with a $119 deductible. There's no additional charge for battery service, but that's only if your battery retains less than 80 percent of its original capacity.
For additional context, an Apple Watch comes with a one-year warranty that covers manufacturer defects, so AppleCare+ is an addition to that standard warranty. For theft or loss, AppleCare+ will only cover you if Find My is enabled when the watch is stolen or lost, and it has to remain enabled throughout the entire claims process.
When AppleCare makes sense, and when to skip it
If you're in a trade, work in construction, play sports or regularly wear your watch in other situations that could cause substantial damage to it, it's much easier to justify coverage. If you're an adrenaline minimalist and the most dangerous part of your day is a run to the convenience store, not so much. Just remember that coverage is protection against a potential expense and far from a guarantee that you'll save money over the long term.
If you can comfortably replace the watch and prefer to set aside the cash, AppleCare+ is not essential. At Apple's current annual rate, three years of premiums come just under $90. If you add a single accidental damage claim, you're at $159. With one theft or loss claim, you've spent $209. Either way, it's a significant portion of the Apple Watch SE's $249 starting cost. And depending on how far into the device's life the damage happens, you might prefer to put the cash toward the next generation instead of repairing an older unit.
Getting a new battery is another reason for potential coverage, but only if you plan on owning and using the same Apple Watch for years. It's basically pointless if you upgrade annually or every two years, as the battery isn't likely to degrade that quickly. If the device is sitting above 80 percent health when you decide to replace the watch's battery, it's not covered.
It's also worth having non-AppleCare repair prices in mind. For the GPS model of the Apple Watch SE 3, you'll pay $99 for battery service and $199 for other damage (there's no theft option without coverage). If you have the cellular model, the damage repair jumps to $229. Your tolerance for these prices affects AppleCare's value.
AppleCare payment plan options
AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss for a single Apple Watch SE 3 is the lowest-cost option among Apple's current Apple Watch models, at $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year. Coverage renews until canceled, and annual billing costs a little less than the $35.88 total you'll pay if you opt for monthly. At three years, the difference amounts to $107.64 total for monthly payments versus $89.97 for annual payments.
AppleCare One is a potential alternative for those with several Apple devices because it lumps them all into a single payment plan, starting at $19.99 monthly for an individual with up to three devices. Add $5.99 per month for each additional device. If you already have three Apple devices, adding an SE 3 will cost more than its standalone $2.99 per month. This only makes sense if you're already paying for AppleCare One and don't have a higher-cost device to protect.
Finally, AppleCare One Family is the newest option. It costs $49.99 for up to six family members and covers all their eligible devices. New Apple products are automatically added to the plan when purchased.
For the base plan, you'll need to enroll in AppleCare+ within 60 days of buying your watch. With the other two plans, you can usually add any devices that are less than four years old to an active plan, though they'll likely require a check to make sure they're in good condition.

title_fa: Discovery+ gets a price bump just a week after the Skydance merger
excerpt_en: Who could have possibly seen this coming.
excerpt_fa: Who could have possibly seen this coming.
content_en:
Discovery+ gets a price bump just a week after the Skydance merger
The ad-free plan now costs $12 per month.
Just a week after Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery officially merged to form Skydance, the company has made Discovery+ more expensive. The ad-supported plan is now $1 pricier at $7 per month, while the ad-free option got a $2 bump up to $12 per month.
The changes took effect on Tuesday for new members. Existing subscribers are getting a 30-day heads-up as the new pricing will kick in with their first bill on or after November 12. The last time Discovery+ prices went up was in January 2025.
Skydance has signaled its intention to combine its other main streaming services — Paramount+ and HBO Max — into a single offering. Perhaps it'll fold Discovery+ into that and have separate tiles or channels for the three, much like Disney+ has for its various brands. In the meantime, at least, Discovery+ subscribers will be paying more to keep using that particular service. More price increases are likely along with cost-cutting measures as Skydance starts addressing the $80 billion pile of debt it has taken on.

title_en: Abu Dhabi will use Ultrahuman's smart ring know-how to boost its public health app
title_fa: Abu Dhabi will use Ultrahuman's smart ring know-how to boost its public health app
excerpt_en: The Abu Dhabi government wants to incorporate wearables data into its public health app.
excerpt_fa: The Abu Dhabi government wants to incorporate wearables data into its public health app.
content_en:
Abu Dhabi will use Ultrahuman's smart ring know-how to boost its public health app
But the system won't mandate the use of Ultrahuman's smart rings.
The Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre is teaming up with Ultrahuman to bring the latter's algorithms to its Sahatna app. Sahatna is the nationwide healthcare app enabling individuals to manage their health, including speaking to doctors and accessing health and genetics records. As of now, the app will also tell users their biological age (as opposed to their chronological age). That comes from Ultrahuman's Ultra Age metric, which analyzes your sleep, cardiovascular and blood markers into a single metric. You won't need to be an Ultrahuman user to get the benefit, as Sahatna's system is device agnostic.
Historically, wearables have received short shrift from doctors and regulators but it's clear the trend is shifting. The ADPHC, for instance, hopes the system will help people gain a better understanding of how lifestyle factors influence their long-term health. It adds that the model, which combines clinical and wearable data, will support "earlier interventions, more targeted prevention strategies and more personalized recommendations." It's not clear at this point if that means officials will be able to target and identify individuals who are deemed to require direct intervention, or if this will be left down to the user.

title_en: X bundles Premium, Grok and Cursor under a single monthly subscription
title_fa: X bundles Premium, Grok and Cursor under a single monthly subscription
excerpt_en: SpaceXSI has announced a new subscription scheme that gives you access to Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium.
excerpt_fa: SpaceXSI has announced a new subscription scheme that gives you access to Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium.
content_en:
X bundles Premium, Grok and Cursor under a single monthly subscription
One membership will give you access to SpaceXSI’s products.
SpaceXSI has announced a unified membership scheme across its products called the X Subscription. The company was formerly known as SpaceXAI until its CEO Elon Musk announced that he would rename it, following President Donald Trump's push to use the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence. An X Subscription plan will include access to Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium, depending on the tier you're paying for. If you'll recall, the company acquired coding startup Cursor back in August.
We've unified plans across Grok, Cursor, and X Premium.
Introducing The X Subscription. pic.twitter.com/SvkrVvBa0p
— SpaceX Super Intelligence (@SpaceXSI) October 12, 2026
The $8-a-month Plus tier for individuals will provide you access to Grok Chat, Voice, Imagine and Build, as well as Grok API and to Cursor for coding. You'll also get X Premium features, including a checkmark, fewer ads on your X timeline, enhanced creator tools and advanced analytics.
Meanwhile, the $30-a-month Premium tier will get you all those, as well as access to Grok Bot and the latest Grok models, the ability to make AI images and videos thru Grok and faster chat responses. On Cursor, you'll get access to code hosting, cloud agents and automations. And on X, you'll get ad-free scrolling and the ability to secure your preferred handle.
The $100-a-month Super tier includes everything in Plus and Premium, along with priority access to Grok models at peak times. Finally, the $200 Ultra tier includes the earliest access to all products and models, as well as 20 times the usage capacity of Plus. The Premium, Super and Ultra plans are also available for teams, while enterprise customers can get customized plans from the company.

title_en: Don't buy a cheap Android phone without these non-negotiable features
title_fa: Don't buy a cheap Android phone without these non-negotiable features
excerpt_en: Android phones can be had at many different price points, but the most important features aren't always found in the cheapest available devices.
excerpt_fa: Android phones can be had at many different price points, but the most important features aren't always found in the cheapest available devices.
content_en:
Don't buy a cheap Android phone without these non-negotiable features
What good is a phone that can't keep up with the average person's day-to-day needs?
You don't have to spend an arm and a leg on an Android phone, even if it's brand-new. You can find plenty of great cheap Android phone options for $300 or less, if you know what to look for. And that's the biggest thing to consider: knowing what features are crucial to have and where you can make concessions. Paying less for a phone that doesn't have a sleek titanium frame, for example, is totally fine; you probably will (and should) put a case on it, anyway. But getting a phone with insufficient RAM, horrible battery life, poor cameras, a bad processor, or a small screen is where you want to draw the line.
In some cases, what you're willing to sacrifice is an individual decision. If you're a casual content creator, for example, the cameras need to be at least above average. But if you're getting a secondary phone for basic messaging, you may be fine with just decent cameras. Nonetheless, there are some non-negotiable limits that anyone seeking out a cheap Android phone should focus on, no matter how you plan to use it.
Screen and RAM minimums
Remember when phones had tiny screens? The original iPhone's 4.5-inch screen seemed groundbreaking at the time, but by today's standards, that just doesn't cut it. A phone should have at least a 5.6-inch screen, though most nowadays are at least 6.1 inches. This allows you to enjoy a comfortable experience when holding the phone and typing two-handed while still being able to clearly see the content on it. That screen should also be an AMOLED panel with HD resolution and a decent peak brightness of at least 1,000 nits, so it's viewable in direct sunlight.
Memory is another factor to consider. You'll want at least 6GB RAM; otherwise, multitasking, video streaming, and casual gaming could be slow or inconsistent, and the phone won't respond quickly enough to your demands. If you play a lot of mobile games, consider even going up to 8GB. Also, if there's no expandable storage (which is a rarity nowadays), 128GB is the minimum you should consider. For peace-of-mind, go with at least 256GB. Otherwise, you'll end up with a "phone full" message before you know it, and you'll be forced to clear out the device or sign up for cloud storage.
Finally, the processor matters. While you might not need the best, fastest, most up-to-date processor, you don't want one that's slow as molasses. Check the age of the processor, as well as reviews for its performance, and factor this into your decision. There's no value in getting a cheap device if it's slow and laggy when you want to stream a movie, and a great processor is vital for gaming on an Android phone.
Don't skimp on the battery and cameras
Battery life and cameras are also important. A battery that's at least 4,500mAh is sufficient, especially if the phone doesn't handle heavy AI processing. But 5,000mAh is a better starting point nowadays to keep you going all day, even with moderate use. With cameras, you want a phone that can at least take photos that are good enough for sharing on social media and keeping for posterity. This means having at least a 32MP sensor for the rear camera, but also a large sensor that can capture more light and yield better photos overall, even if the megapixels are lower in one camera versus another. Don't discount the front sensor and resolution as well, as this is what you'll use to take selfies. Look for at least a 12MP front camera with, again, a good sensor size.
Consider other basics like NFC for tap-to-pay and more recent Bluetooth versions for reliable connectivity to headphones and speakers. For older models, confirm that there's at least a few years left of software and security support. This sounds like a lot, but you'll find plenty of devices that fit, like Samsung's Galaxy A series phones (see our review of the Samsung Galaxy A17, for example) and phones from brands like Nothing and Motorola.
Even older-model Google Pixel phones can fit the criteria. You can find a renewed Google Pixel 8a for just over $300 nowadays, and it comes with just about every vital feature mentioned previously. Ideally, wait for seasonal promotions to find a decked-out mid-range phone for the price of a budget one. You'll have to make compromises to go cheap, but there are many phones in the $300 range that meet or exceed non-negotiable features and specs.

title_en: How to boost your GPU performance without buying a new one
title_fa: How to boost your GPU performance without buying a new one
excerpt_en: With an older GPU, you'll need to go without some of the fancy features, but you can still enjoy high frame rates with the right changes.
excerpt_fa: With an older GPU, you'll need to go without some of the fancy features, but you can still enjoy high frame rates with the right changes.
content_en:
How to boost your GPU performance without buying a new one
Your old GPU might not be able to compete with a new card, but it can run better with some tweaks.
In this increasingly anti-consumer tech world that seems fixed on abandoning all else in favor of data centers, there's rarely been a worse time to buy a new GPU. While many panic-bought PCs to avoid RAMaggedon, there's an even bigger crowd of PC gamers who have been unable to pick up a new graphics card for years.
Just because you're unable to afford a shiny NVIDIA RTX 50-Series GPU doesn't mean you can't squeeze more performance out of your current card, though. Some graphics tweaks, supersampling advice and general GPU maintenance will help boost FPS performance in your favorite games.
Use supersampling and frame generation to boost FPS
In an era where graphical advancements are outpacing hardware evolution — hello, path tracing — it's becoming vital to get the most out of your current GPU through any means necessary. As someone who is now smitten with high-end ray tracing (it looks incredible in the likes of Cyberpunk 2077 or Marvel's Spider-Man 2), I'm all about embracing AI to help boost frame rates. And yes, I do need to give my soul a shower for admitting that.
Whether you're interested in advanced ray tracing features or not, it's clear that graphically demanding games now rely on various forms of supersampling to lock down buttery, console-beating frame rates. Be it AMD FSR, NVIDIA DLSS or Intel XeSS, making the most out of AI-driven, FPS-boosting tech can be crucial for maintaining stable performance at high resolutions. None of us can be snobs when it comes to supersampling or frame generation now.
Both NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 and AMD FSR 4 produce image quality that's on par with playing games at native resolution, while drastically boosting performance. These technologies work by rendering a game at a lower internal resolution (thus producing fewer pixels) before using deep learning techniques to upscale the final image to a far higher pixel count. Since DLSS 2.0 launched back in 2020, I have leaned on supersampling. With the current iterations of the big three solutions, it basically means free frames with little downside.
The issue of NVIDIA's DLSS 4.5 Multi Frame Generation tech is a little more complicated. While it's capable of producing 200 fps-topping results in Hogwarts Legacy with the x6 modifier enabled in my experience, it adds serious input latency in games that support the fledgling technology. Earlier incarnations of Team Green's tech that top out at x2 and x3 modifiers perform nicely on supported titles, with the added benefit of producing fewer distracting visual artifacts than MFG (like shimmering around in-game text).
As a PC player of 30 years, I can recommend supersampling without hesitation. Regarding the pros and cons of frame gen, I suggest experimenting with it until you make up your own mind.
Lower settings and turn off ray tracing
This is an obvious one, but if your GPU is sputtering away and dropping frames in the best PC games, it's best to lower graphical settings right away. Only the fastest graphics cards can cope with a modern AAA title's Ultra preset, so unless you're rocking a top-tier card, it's wise to drop your settings to Balanced. If your GPU is a couple of generations old, selecting a game's Performance preset should help you claw back even more frames at the cost of graphical fidelity.
Unless you've got an ultra-obsessive eye, it's unlikely you're going to miss features like ambient occlusion or screen space reflections. By all means, tinker with in-game sliders to see what you like the look of and whether you can stomach the resulting performance cost.
In high-octane first-person shooters or fast-paced racing games, fancy rendering techniques are wasted on most gamers. Do yourself a favor and disable any setting that doesn't enhance your experience. An increasing number of PC titles (like Resident Evil Requiem) have excellent graphics menus that provide before and after shots of how effects alter a game. If you can't appreciate the difference in these preview panes, shut the setting off to improve your chances of boosting fps.
Those on budget GPUs should never enable ray tracing. This ultra-advanced lighting technique uses multi-bounce illumination to create incredibly realistic in-game shadows and reflections, but it's hugely punishing on performance. Unless you own a beastly graphics card, ray tracing should almost always be disabled, as it can often lower frame rates by some 20 to 40 percent.
Remember the basics, clean your GPU and consider overclocking
Though the above methods should help pump up your frame rate numbers, there's a physical element to this as well. You must know how to clean and organize your PC properly to get the most out of it. Keeping the inside of your system tidy can be a surprising way to up its effectiveness.
Thermal throttling is a potentially big issue for both your GPU and CPU. If you don't regularly maintain your machine, dust can quickly build up, leading to a situation where the pride and joy of your gaming PC can't maintain a regular airflow. Dust gathering around the fans of a GPU can lead to decreased performance as your card hits its temperature limit more quickly. Once it does, core clock speeds will reduce in order to lower temps, resulting in reduced frame rates.
To safely clean your graphics card, first switch off your PC and unplug it. Once you gain access to your GPU, you'll want a can of compressed air and a soft microfiber cloth on hand. Use short spurts of air directed at the fans to disperse debris, then give the card a gentle wipe with the cloth. This isn't a guaranteed FPS booster, but it will at least keep your GPU in good (hopefully optimal) shape going forward.
Don't neglect the basics, either. Keep your GPU driver updated for the best performance, and close as many background apps as possible so your system isn't devoting...

title_en: How to turn your old hard drives into a RAID array
title_fa: How to turn your old hard drives into a RAID array
excerpt_en: Your old hard drives still have some live left in them.
excerpt_fa: Your old hard drives still have some live left in them.
content_en:
How to turn your old hard drives into a RAID array
Your old hard drives still have some life left in them.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Cloud storage is everywhere. Despite the ongoing memory crisis, SSDs have gotten cheap enough that most new PCs don't even bother with a spinning drive anymore. And yet, if you build your own computers, there's a good chance you've got a drawer of old 500GB and 1TB hard drives that are too small to be useful on their own but still coule have some life left in them. RAID is what you do with that drawer. Rather than throwing these hard drives away, RAID can give them a new purpose. Plus, it gives you faster and more reliable storage.
What is a RAID array?
RAID stands for Redundant Array of Independent Disks. The idea here is to combine multiple disks so they function as a single unit. Instead of storing your files on a single drive, RAID distributes them across two or more disks, which results in much faster transfer speeds. They won't match the speeds of an SSD, but they're much faster than a conventional HDD. A RAID array also provides redundancy for your data. That's because it's less prone to failure — if one drive fails, you can still recover your files from the other one. That's the main reason why RAID is still used today. It's less about the faster speeds and more about convenience and reliability.
A RAID system doesn't replace a full backup, but it does ensure that you won't lose your data if one of your hard drives fails completely. The idea sounds great, but there are many details you need to know before setting up your own RAID array. For instance, there are four different categories of RAID arrays. Each one drastically changes the results you'll get when combining your disks. The best-known ones are RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5 and RAID 10. Understanding each of them is very important so you know exactly what to expect.
Understanding the different RAID levels
RAID 0 essentially combines two or more disks into a single unit without parity. This process, known as striping, speeds up file read and write times. It can be very useful if you work with large files, such as videos or databases, because it combines the total storage space of all the drives. But it's not all good news. The downside is that RAID 0 offers zero data protection. If a drive fails, you lose everything. In short, it's a great way to get faster speeds, but not so great for keeping your data safe.
If you need something more reliable, there's RAID 1. With this setup, the system writes exactly the same data to every disk in the array. If one of the disks fails or disconnects, you'll still have everything on the other one. No need to worry about losing your data — perfect for when you're working on an important project. They usually come with a RAID chip built in, so all you need to do is plug the drives into it. Just be sure to check the maximum capacities and speeds before buying one. It's the same as choosing USB-C accessories — high speeds aren't guaranteed for all of them.

title_en: How to use Google Gemini to automate tasks
title_fa: How to use Google Gemini to automate tasks
excerpt_en: Spark is Google's AI tool that can perform tasks on your behalf.
excerpt_fa: Spark is Google's AI tool that can perform tasks on your behalf.
content_en:
How to use Google Gemini to automate tasks
Spark is Google's AI tool that can perform tasks on your behalf.
One of AI's promises, on the less "humanity-destroying" end of the spectrum, is to make everyday life a little smoother. Instead of tackling each item on your to-do list by yourself, perhaps a reliable AI tool could cross a few entries off for you, leaving you to attend to the more important bits. Getting a recap of the last 20 emails in your inbox might let you dive into your work faster in the mornings, or at least give you a couple of extra minutes to stare into the middle distance while sipping your coffee.
If you're committed to the Google ecosystem, Gemini Spark might offer a way to automate the tasks you'd rather farm out. Spark is an agentic personal assistant announced in May at Google's annual I/O developer conference. You can give it a task, and it can run in the background, taking what Google describes as "proactive action," while still adhering to your instructions.
The Gemini Spark website gives a few examples of what you can do with it, like turning your last 50 email responses into a style guide covering how you answer emails, or setting up a tracker for internships. It's integrated into Google Workspace apps like Docs, Calendar, Slides and Gmail, as well as Personal Intelligence, a feature Gemini uses to customize suggestions based on information from your Google apps.
Here's how to use Gemini Spark to automate tasks.
Before you start
To access Gemini Spark, you'll need to be a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber. Certain business subscribers might also have access. (You also can't be located in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the UK or Nigeria.) You'll also need "Keep activity" switched on, which the company says "lets you pick up chats where you left off." Spark is available through the Gemini mobile app, the Gemini Mac app and the web app. Spark also works with Gemini in Chrome using auto browse to do tasks like book restaurant reservations, travel and the like.
Aside from the basics of getting set up, Google also has some words of caution. As glorious as it would be to just set it and forget it, it's worth the reminder that AI can still make mistakes, so keep an eye on whatever tasks you've set up. Google itself also warns not to put sensitive information into the task thread. That means you shouldn't be giving Gemini login or payment information. Instead, Google recommends entering that type of info yourself directly on the relevant website. Google also cautions against scheduling tasks that are too sensitive, particularly if the task is set to run while you're offline. Consider whether a mistake like a hallucination could cause actual harm.
How to create a task
Whether you're on the mobile or web app, select Menu, and then select Spark. Then, you can type into the textbox whatever task you want Spark to accomplish. The Spark website gives this prompt, for example: "When I receive an email inquiring about my photography services, automatically extract the client's name, requested date, and log the lead in my 'Client Tracker' Sheet. Then create a new Google Drive folder named after the client." If needed, it's at this point that you can also upload a relevant file, or something from your Drive or a Notebook. Then, tap or click Submit.
Google emphasizes monitoring your tasks in case Gemini needs something from you, like taking over a task in the browser. To keep an eye on your tasks, once again go to Menu > Spark and then Tasks. That will let you see the thread associated with the task, and if you need to make updates, you can do it right there. You can also look at the work panel, which shows you information like the completed, current and planned steps, by tapping the progress chip at the top of the thread.
At the end of September, Google said it would replace Gemini Gems with skills as the method for dictating instructions for tasks. In a blog post, the company described how you can use skills to automate repetitive tasks. A skill might be instructions for preparing for presentations or adopting a specific writing style. Google said that once you've created a skill, if you want to use it again on a task, you'll be able to type a forward slash and the skill's name when you're writing your prompt.

title_en: Why are your iPhone photos so blurry (and how to improve it)
title_fa: Why are your iPhone photos so blurry (and how to improve it)
excerpt_en: Blurry iPhone photos can come down to more than just a dirty lens. Here's how to expertly sharpen your shots and fine-tune your camera settings.
excerpt_fa: Blurry iPhone photos can come down to more than just a dirty lens. Here's how to expertly sharpen your shots and fine-tune your camera settings.
content_en:
Why are your iPhone photos so blurry (and how to improve it)
Blurry photos usually go deeper than a little grease on your lens.
Phone cameras are a modern convenience that's all too often taken for granted, making casual photography accessible to millions in a lightweight package. While your phone's camera probably won't beat out a device designed exclusively for taking photos and video, there are ways to take some especially pretty pictures with just your smartphone. That makes it all the more cumbersome when those pictures come out blurry — an all-too-common problem for iPhone users.
While any phone can take a blurry photo, the proliferation of the iPhone has led most complaints of this sort to center on it. Luckily, the iPhone has an incredible number of camera settings, including a whole host of ways to avoid blurry pictures — and you won't even need the fancy AI Clean Up tools from iOS 27 for great results. Whether it's making sure your lens is clean or turning on the right toggles for dark video, blurry photos are easy to fix.
Why your iPhone photos might be blurry
Before messing with any settings, you'll want to make sure your camera lens isn't what's causing the issue. If your lens is smudged up, don't just dab it with tissue paper or the end of your shirt; take off the case, grab a microfiber cloth, and wipe the lens down. If marks are persistent, add a very light dab of distilled water to the cloth (not right on the lens!) and wipe gently.
That's just the tip of the iceberg, though, as a lot of iPhone footage and photos can still turn out blocky or blurry, lacking the crispness you might be looking for. The next issue you want to look at is the light level you're working with, which is a prime culprit behind so many blurry shots. Low light levels make it harder for cameras to focus reliably, often require slower shutter speeds, and can introduce more noise — all of which can leave photos and videos looking blurry, grainy, or blocky after compression. If you want to improve your smartphone photography, you'll need to deal with low-light conditions.
Which settings to change for less blurry photos and videos
A good start is the camera settings on your iPhone (Settings > Camera), where you can change the resolution at the top (there are different frame rates and resolution settings here, but anything above 720p will generally produce crisper image quality). However, some of the more helpful features are in the camera itself, such as locking focus: Instead of letting your camera shift focus all over the place, you can tap the image and hold on the area you want to focus on until the "AE/AF LOCK" prompt appears on-screen. On models iPhone 11 and newer, you can also turn on Night Mode (signified by the moon icon at the top of the camera interface), though it will turn on automatically if you're in low light. Night Mode will automatically brighten and capture low-light images with more detail.
When it comes to adjusting shutter speeds and changing your ISO settings — slower shutter speeds can introduce motion blur, while higher ISO settings can increase visible noise and reduce image quality — you'll need a third-party app like Camera+. Apps like these let you dig into the minute controls of your camera and give you a leg up if you're on an older device. In addition to digital tools, you should consider getting a tripod to stabilize your shots if you're serious about avoiding blur. A tripod keeps the iPhone still during longer exposures, reducing camera shake that can otherwise turn small movements into visible blur — especially in low light.

title_en: The Social Reckoning is flopping at the box office
title_fa: The Social Reckoning is flopping at the box office
excerpt_en: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron's Sorkin's follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that's...
excerpt_fa: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron's Sorkin's follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that's...
content_en:
As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron’s Sorkin’s follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that’s somewhere within the $30–42 million range. That would make it a certifiable flop that’s costing Columbia Pictures (and Sony) quite a bit of money — especially when you compare it to The Social Network’s $22 million opening.
The Social Reckoning is flopping at the box office
Meanwhile, Other Mommy is having an unexpected moment.
Meanwhile, Other Mommy is having an unexpected moment.
This isn’t entirely surprising given how middling reviews for the film have been. It’s currently got a 55% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and has widely been trashed on social media. All of this might be reflective of audiences hoping for a proper sequel to The Social Network, which won three Oscars for its screenplay (written by Sorkin), editing, and score. But it might speak to people not fully clicking with Mikey Madison’s performance as whistleblower Frances Haugen or Jeremy Allen White’s turn as Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. (Madison, for her part, indicated to The Hollywood Reporter that it was Sorkin’s vision as director that kept from “authentically and faithfully represent[ing] a real person,” which she hopes to do in the future.) It also probably didn’t help that Jesse Eisenberg — who portrayed Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network — had no interest in being in the film, according to Sorkin himself.
Ironically, Blumhouse’s Other Mommy raked in an impressive $27.5 million this weekend, which likely suggests that people are more interested in novel horror as opposed to reminders of how social media has made everyone’s lives worse.

title_en: Epic reportedly delays its Disney video game so it can be made using more AI
title_fa: Epic reportedly delays its Disney video game so it can be made using more AI
excerpt_en: Developers were apparently ordered to use AI for both code and asset creation.
excerpt_fa: Developers were apparently ordered to use AI for both code and asset creation.
content_en:
Epic reportedly delays its Disney video game so it can be made using more AI
That’s certainly a choice.
Epic Games is going all in on AI for game development. The studio has been working on games for Disney, but sources told Bloomberg that its upcoming release has been delayed in order to use more AI for its creation. The publication reported that one of the game's directors informed the team that the project would be adopting an "AI first" production plan. "No more hand-written code," the internal message stated, as well as ordering all art for the project to be "generated with full AI workflows."
The publication's sources said this new approach was not universally well-received by the devs, with some employees allegedly hoping that the request wasn't totally serious. However, Epic Games has already been pushing a lot of generative AI tools into its Unreal Engine platform this year, so the directive seems pretty real. "We're embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," Epic's Communications Director Jake Jones said in a statement to Bloomberg.
Disney announced a hefty investment of $1.5 billion into Epic back in 2024. While several Disney-owned characters have appeared as Fortnite skins over the years, this deeper collaboration was aimed at creating a "games and entertainment universe." Earlier this year, it was rumored that the developer's most promising project for Disney was an extraction shooter a la Arc Raiders. That game was purportedly due to launch in November, although Bloomberg's latest report was that the date had been pushed back to March even before the new AI mission was given.
According to GDC's annual survey, a growing number of devs see gen AI as bad for the business. Fifty-two percent said the tech was bad for the industry in this year's survey, up from 30 percent in 2025. The survey also revealed that while many in gaming do use gen AI tools, it's primarily for tasks such as research and programming rather than asset creation.

title_en: Meta says it's caught up to the frontier with its latest Wonder AI models
title_fa: Meta says it's caught up to the frontier with its latest Wonder AI models
excerpt_en: The models add "active memory" and "active focus" abilities.
excerpt_fa: The models add "active memory" and "active focus" abilities.
content_en:
Meta says it's caught up to the frontier with its latest Wonder AI models
The models add "active memory" and "active focus" abilities.
After spending more than a year and tens of billions of dollars rebuilding its AI efforts, Meta says that it has caught up with the frontier. The company introduced its two latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, both of which represent "a major leap toward personal superintelligence."
According to Meta, the models are particularly adept at navigating legal, financial and health-related tasks, and are able to deliver "frontier coding performance." Both models also add "active memory" and "active focus," which Meta says will help people accomplish more over long periods of time.
That's notable because Meta says it plans to bring Wonder to its personal agent Muse, beginning with paid subscribers. Active memory, according to the company, is "the ability to carry what matters to you across conversations and bring back the details that are relevant to the task at hand" while active focus will allow an agent to "keep working toward your goal when a task gets hard."
The models are a notable milestone for Meta, which has said it expects to spend as much as $145 billion this year to fuel its ambitious AI plans. In an interview with the Financial Times, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that "getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work" from the company's superintelligence team.
The new models are rolling out now to subscribers. Muse Wonder is available via Meta's API and in Muse Code. It's priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Muse Wonder Full is available to people who subscribe to the $50/month "power usage" or $200/month "maximum usage" tiers of Muse Code.

The models add "active memory" and "active focus" abilities.
After spending more than a year and tens of billions of dollars rebuilding its AI efforts, Meta says that it has caught up with the frontier. The company introduced its two latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, both of which represent "a major leap toward personal superintelligence."
According to Meta, the models are particularly adept at navigating legal, financial and health-related tasks, and are able to deliver "frontier coding performance." Both models also add "active memory" and "active focus," which Meta says will help people accomplish more over long periods of time.
That's notable because Meta says it plans to bring Wonder to its personal agent Muse, beginning with paid subscribers. Active memory, according to the company, is "the ability to carry what matters to you across conversations and bring back the details that are relevant to the task at hand" while active focus will allow an agent to "keep working toward your goal when a task gets hard."
The models are a notable milestone for Meta, which has said it expects to spend as much as $145 billion this year to fuel its ambitious AI plans. In an interview with the Financial Times, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that "getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work" from the company's superintelligence team.
The new models are rolling out now to subscribers. Muse Wonder is available via Meta's API and in Muse Code. It's priced at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Muse Wonder Full is available to people who subscribe to the $50/month "power usage" or $200/month "maximum usage" tiers of Muse Code.

title_en: Norway fined a Microsoft subsidiary $9.6 million for allegedly misusing Grindr user data
title_fa: Norway fined a Microsoft subsidiary $9.6 million for allegedly misusing Grindr user data
excerpt_en: Xandr has three weeks to appeal the record penalty.
excerpt_fa: Xandr has three weeks to appeal the record penalty.
content_en:
Norway fined a Microsoft subsidiary $9.6 million for allegedly misusing Grindr user data
Xandr has three weeks to appeal the record penalty.
The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (NDPA) has charged Xandr, an adtech subsidiary of Microsoft, with a fine of 92 million Norwegian kroner, or around $9.6 million. According to the data protection agency, Xandr allegedly didn't obtain "explicit consent" to use sensitive user data of those on Grindr for advertising purposes, instead only assuming that the dating app already secured user approval. It's also the highest fine that the Norwegian authority has issued to date.
"When a person opened Grindr, their personal data was in many cases relayed through Xandr to potentially thousands of actors in the advertising ecosystem," the NDPA wrote in a press release. "Advertisers could thereby bid against each other to present targeted adverts, completely hidden from the individual user."
The case started in 2020 when the country's consumer council filed a complaint against Xandr, which wasn't owned by Microsoft at the time, with the NDPA. The complaint accused Xandr of unlawfully sharing users' personal data for commercial purposes without getting consent first. The Norwegian data authority justified the "high fine in this case" due to the data misuse that it considered "very serious." The NDPA said the fine was calculated from Xandr's total annual turnover and that the data infringements took place between July 2018 and April 2020.
While Xandr is the accused offender in this case, Grindr has itself been involved in cases of improperly sharing sensitive user data. Previously, the same Norwegian agency charged the dating app with a more than 5.6 million euro fine, or around $6.2 million, for similar reasons. Grindr was also hit with a lawsuit in London in 2024 for allegedly sharing data that included the HIV status and test dates of its users.
