title_en: Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
title_fa: Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
excerpt_en: The RG DDS's main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
excerpt_fa: The RG DDS's main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
content_en:
Anbernic's next dual-screen handheld has the perfect aspect ratio for 3DS games
The RG DDS’s main display has a 5:3 aspect ratio while its bottom screen will be 4:3.
It's only been a year since Anbernic teased its remake of the Nintendo DS but the handheld company is already moving on to a contemporary version of its successor. Anbernic revealed the RG DDS, which is short for "Dream Dual-Screen" and an obvious nod to the Nintendo 3DS.
Improving on its predecessor, the RG DS, Anbernic went with Qualcomm's Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 chip. That means the RG DDS should handle emulating even up to Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 2 titles. Equipped with two displays, most gamers are likely going to replay 3DS favorites because of its matching aspect ratios. Anbernic built the clamshell handheld with a 4.7-inch main display that has a 1,200 x 720 resolution for a 5:3 aspect ratio and paired it with a 4-inch secondary display with a 960 x 720 resolution for a 4:3 aspect ratio. Anbernic hasn't revealed the rest of its upcoming handheld's internals, outside having a 6,000mAh battery.
As for the controls, the RG DDS is almost an exact match to Nintendo's handheld, but Anbernic added an extra analog stick on the right side. The dual-screen device even has an extendable capacitive stylus that can be tucked away when not in use. Anbernic also said there's a dedicated AI button, but hasn't yet detailed exactly what features it activates.
As usual, the handheld maker excluded any pricing or release dates in the reveal, but we're expecting the RG DDS to be a little more expensive than its $99 precursor. However, Anbernic is known for its affordability so it could potentially undercut the recently-released Retroid Pocket Duo and its Lite model that starts at $149.

title_en: The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
title_fa: The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
excerpt_en: Sure, you can set your iPhone's alarm to any time you choose. But there's a hidden limit to how far your choices will stretch, though most users won't reach it.
excerpt_fa: Sure, you can set your iPhone's alarm to any time you choose. But there's a hidden limit to how far your choices will stretch, though most users won't reach it.
content_en:
The iPhone clock app has an oddity not many people know about
There’s a limit to how far your alarm settings will scroll, and most people never reach it.
The iPhone Clock app has been around since the original iPhone launched 19 years ago, and for most, it's always been a fairly straightforward default app. However, there's a small curiosity hiding within the alarm settings that went viral in mid-2025, along with another quirk we'll talk about below. To put it simply, the alarm hour and minute scrolls seem infinite at first glance, but rapidly scrolling through the hours and minutes will eventually reach a dead end at 4:39. For those with a preference for military time, it ends at 16:39. Go ahead, give it a try and see for yourself.
Open the Clock app, select Alarms, tap the + button and start scrolling through the hours and minutes until you reach the end. It will take several swipes, but not too many if you scroll through as fast as you can, which is the reason why most people never noticed it in the first place. However, this little endpoint doesn't mean you're limited in setting alarms.
So why does the iPhone alarm stop at 4:39? The specific hour and minute seem a little strange and random, right? Well, Apple hasn't weighed in on this, but reports and online discussions offer differing explanations, like something called Tableview that an X user thinks is involved. For the most part, just treat it as an interesting idiosyncrasy. The numbers don't add up to 23 or anything, so there's no need to delve into conspiracy theories.
The icon tells time
Who knew? But seriously, there's another little detail here that's easier to spot once you know where to look. The Clock app icon isn't static. It tells you the current time, including a moving second hand. Apple introduced this feature in iOS 7, back when we were still grunting and finger painting on cave walls. If you've always opened the app to look at the time, you never really had to.
Also, there's an even subtler feature alluded to in the opening paragraph. Normally, the second hand moves in a continuous "sweeping" motion all the way around. On iOS 26.1 devices and later, however, Low Power Mode changes the motion to a once-per-second tick, like a traditional quartz clock. It still tells the time, of course, only with a less fluid animation. This is only a visual change, and there's no audible ticking involved.
If you're looking for one more option that's hidden in plain sight, open Stopwatch inside the iPhone Clock app and swipe across the display. You can switch between digital and analog stopwatch faces without installing another app. Unlike the alarm's endpoint, this is a documented feature that's included in the iPhone user guide.
How do I change the appearance of the clock app on my iPhone?
Now that the Clock's dirty laundry is out in the open, how about changing the app's appearance? Both the worst and the best iPhones offer a few clock-display options, though they're far from the aesthetic variety offered by other apps.
If you want a large bedside alarm clock, connect your iPhone to a charger and stand it up on its side. This places it in StandBy mode, which displays widgets, photos or just a good old-fashioned clock. Change the types of clocks displayed by swiping to the left or right.
Last but not least, you can enable Night Mode so StandBy mode adapts to the low-light environment of a typical bedroom when it's sleepy time. The screen will display a heavy red tint, so it's a little less intrusive, especially if the bedside table is level with your face. It's not a mysterious oddity or anything, but there it is.
However, if you expect your iPhone to behave exactly like a standard bedside clock, you'll need to make sure Always-On Display is active in Settings. It works best to slap a MagSafe charger with a kickstand on the back. Some older iPhones don't have Always-On Display, so you'll have to give the screen a little nudge to turn it on or you can pester Siri about it.

So why does the iPhone alarm stop at 4:39? The specific hour and minute seem a little strange and random, right? Well, Apple hasn't weighed in on this, but reports and online discussions offer differing explanations, like something called Tableview that an X user thinks is involved. For the most part, just treat it as an interesting idiosyncrasy. The numbers don't add up to 23 or anything, so there's no need to delve into conspiracy theories.
The icon tells time
Who knew? But seriously, there's another little detail here that's easier to spot once you know where to look. The Clock app icon isn't static. It tells you the current time, including a moving second hand. Apple introduced this feature in iOS 7, back when we were still grunting and finger painting on cave walls. If you've always opened the app to look at the time, you never really had to.
Also, there's an even subtler feature alluded to in the opening paragraph. Normally, the second hand moves in a continuous "sweeping" motion all the way around. On iOS 26.1 devices and later, however, Low Power Mode changes the motion to a once-per-second tick, like a traditional quartz clock. It still tells the time, of course, only with a less fluid animation. This is only a visual change, and there's no audible ticking involved.
If you're looking for one more option that's hidden in plain sight, open Stopwatch inside the iPhone Clock app and swipe across the display. You can switch between digital and analog stopwatch faces without installing another app. Unlike the alarm's endpoint, this is a documented feature that's included in the iPhone user guide.
How do I change the appearance of the clock app on my iPhone?
Now that the Clock's dirty laundry is out in the open, how about changing the app's appearance? Both the worst and the best iPhones offer a few clock-display options, though they're far from the aesthetic variety offered by other apps.
If you want a large bedside alarm clock, connect your iPhone to a charger and stand it up on its side. This places it in StandBy mode, which displays widgets, photos or just a good old-fashioned clock. Change the types of clocks displayed by swiping to the left or right.
Last but not least, you can enable Night Mode so StandBy mode adapts to the low-light environment of a typical bedroom when it's sleepy time. The screen will display a heavy red tint, so it's a little less intrusive, especially if the bedside table is level with your face. It's not a mysterious oddity or anything, but there it is.
However, if you expect your iPhone to behave exactly like a standard bedside clock, you'll need to make sure Always-On Display is active in Settings. It works best to slap a MagSafe charger with a kickstand on the back. Some older iPhones don't have Always-On Display, so you'll have to give the screen a little nudge to turn it on or you can pester Siri about it.

title_en: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
title_fa: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
excerpt_en: When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling...
excerpt_fa: When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," you'd be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley's most powerful are falling...
content_en:
When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” you’d be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the great AI rebrand he so desires.
Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand.
Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand.
That Elon Musk was quick to jump on board, promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn’t surprising. When, hours after Donald Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Marc Benioff announced that Salesforce would rename AIForce to SIForce; it seemed like a quick capitulation, but not entirely out of character.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attended the summit where the executive order requiring government agencies to use the term “super intelligence” was announced. He’s also aligned himself with Trump, saying he believes the danger posed by AI is overblown. So it was somewhat predictable that when Nvidia declared that it would “commit” $1 billion to scientific advancement, that included “super intelligence research.” Of course, Huang has a lot to lose if he gets on Trump’s bad side.
The latest to cave is Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, who attended the same AI summit as Huang along with Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jeff Bezos, Dario Amodei, and Musk. In a post calling for building an “emergency brake” for AI yesterday, Nadella repeatedly referred to the technology as “super intelligence.”
During Trump’s second term, Silicon Valley has repeatedly tried to ingratiate itself with the administration, after having a much more contentious relationship during his first term.

title_en: Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
title_fa: Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
excerpt_en: In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
excerpt_fa: In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
content_en:
Steam Frame teardown reveals one problem with its future repairs
In an otherwise repairable device, the cooling fan is hard to reach.
Although the Steam Frame is too expensive and late to the party to bring the masses into VR, it does a lot of things right. That includes its repairability. But iFixit's teardown flagged one component that isn't easy enough to reach: the cooling fan.
The problem? That fan is buried deep inside the headset. To get to it, you have to snake past the optical assemblies, making your way through a dense jungle of thermal hardware, cables and other components. While the fan and heat pipe are separate (a good thing), getting there in the first place is more of a problem.
That's a lot of disassembly for a part that may need cleaning over time. After all, fans accumulate dust, and they eventually wear out. Burying one this deep makes the Steam Frame a harder repair than it otherwise might have been.
A blemish on an otherwise smooth repair path
Fortunately, repairs elsewhere are a much more encouraging story. The Steam Frame's head strap detaches via quick-release latches, making it easier to work on the rear battery pack without messing with the displays. In a win for hygiene, the sweat-absorbing parts are replaceable, including the nose bridge and face and headrest cushions.
The lenses attach magnetically to the headset's IPD rail, making display and eye tracking repairs relatively straightforward. (Removing them does still require some disassembly, including screws and cables.) Overall, it's a fairly approachable repair by VR standards. No digging out the motherboard required.
There are a few other catches. The headset's battery lacks release tabs. (iFixit removed it using isopropyl alcohol and some gentle prying.) In addition, the controllers' thumbsticks are soldered to their boards, so replacing a broken one would be more involved than you might hope.
You'll eventually be able to buy replacement parts from iFixit's store. (Although iFixit is also Valve's repair partner, it says the headset maker had no input on the teardown or editorial process.) However, the company says replacement batteries won't be available when its Steam Frame parts store goes live. That seems like a pretty big omission, and it's one that iFixit says it hopes to change. Replacement displays also won't be available at launch. Of course, Valve does offer warranty repairs and replacements for covered devices, but that doesn't negate the importance of DIY support.
Can't fix that price
Overall, iFixit's teardown reveals a surprisingly repairable VR headset. But whether you want to buy one is another matter. Starting at $1,059, the Steam Frame costs considerably more than the Meta Quest 3. And it does so without delivering an equivalently upgraded experience.
To be fair, it is a powerful and comfortable headset with many perks. It has standalone support for many Steam games, including the excellent Half-Life: Alyx. It also offers wireless PC streaming and microSD expansion. But on the whole, it feels like a headset that would have made more sense several years ago, when developers were investing more resources in VR software. The Steam Frame's high price (thanks, RAMageddon!) combined with that late arrival makes it a tough sell, despite the solid repairability.
You can read more about the Steam Frame in Devindra Hardawar's review.

title_en: The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
title_fa: The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
excerpt_en: Digital game licenses aren't perfect, which is why you might see a padlock icon blocking you from PS5 games.
excerpt_fa: Digital game licenses aren't perfect, which is why you might see a padlock icon blocking you from PS5 games.
content_en:
The meaning behind the padlock symbol in your PlayStation 5 game library
Being locked out of your own games isn't fun, but there are solutions to get back in.
Sony's plans to stop making disc-based games beginning in January 2028 mean digital games need to work flawlessly. Unfortunately, that's not always the case. On your PS5, you may have found some titles inaccessible, as evidenced by a padlock icon over their thumbnails. From your perspective, this can be baffling. You've paid for a game and installed it, so it should always be ready to play, right?
The reality is that when you buy a game from an online store, you typically don't get permanent ownership rights — just a license to download and play. Sony has final control over how you access games associated with your account. If the company withdraws a license for whatever reason, or something goes wrong with the authentication process, you're blocked from accessing the title. This is what the padlock indicates.
As if that weren't enough, the way PlayStation Store and Plus subscriptions work can create headaches. Thankfully, there are some methods to fix those padlocks.
Fixing the PlayStation padlock icon
First, check that you're signed into the right PlayStation account, since that's what ties all your purchases and subscriptions together. You can sign out of an account by going to Settings > Users and Accounts > Other > Sign Out, or sign back in via Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Sign in. This menu lets you create new accounts if needed, too. Next, confirm that PlayStation Network is online using the PlayStation Status page. If PSN is down, you may get locked out of games.
You'll also want to verify that PSN recognizes your purchases, or in the case of PlayStation Plus, that you both have an active subscription and the game you want to play is included with it. Titles are added and removed on a regular basis, so you'll see a padlock on games you previously downloaded that aren't in the library anymore (as well as if your subscription has lapsed).
Scan your transaction history at Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Payment and Subscriptions > Transaction History. As for Plus, your status is under Settings > Users and Accounts > Account > Payment and Subscriptions > Subscriptions, and you can browse the PlayStation Plus website for the current library.
When multiple people share a console, it's possible to play another person's games under your own account. This is known as "gamesharing," and works as long the owner has Console Sharing and Offline Play enabled under Settings > Users and Accounts > Other. That option can only be enabled on one PS5 at a time per account, so if the owner has multiple consoles, they may need to re-designate the one you're on.
If you know you should have direct or shared access to a game, you may need to force PSN to restore licenses. Go to the game in your library, press the Options button on your controller, then select Restore License. You can also go to Settings > Users and Accounts > Other > Restore Licenses to fix multiple games simultaneously.
What if your PS5 games are still locked up?
Before moving forward, restart your PS5 (press the PS Button on your controller, then go to the Power menu and choose Restart PS5). You should also install any available updates at Settings > System > System Software > System Software Update and Settings. Bugs fixed by the latest patches don't typically affect licensing issues, but it's good to rule everything out.
Finally, if you see the padlock icon on a disc-based game, that means the disc isn't acting as a "key" to authenticate the title. Confirm sure the correct disc is inserted into your console. Eject it and make sure it's clean and inserted the right way (label facing up if the console is horizontal, or to the left if it's vertical).
Beyond these, in an extreme scenario, there could be a glitch with your PS5's database. You can attempt to solve this by booting your console into Safe Mode. Follow these steps:
- Turn off the system by holding the Power button on its front until you hear a second beep, which takes a few seconds.
- Once the console shuts down, press and keep holding the Power button again. Release it only after you hear two beeps, the second of which should trigger in seven seconds.
- Connect your controller via a USB cable, then press the PS Button on the controller.
- Once Safe Mode is running, select Clear Cache and Rebuild Database.
Should that not accomplish anything, it's time to talk to PlayStation Support.

content_en:
The latest rumors are that the new Apple TV will have a built-in microphone, while the upgraded remote will get a speaker. The mic would let users control the set-top box using Siri without having to speak into the remote or a connected HomePod device. That could also let the Apple TV serve as a simple smart home hub — controlling thermostats and locking doors — without the need to hunt for the remote.
The new Apple TV could have a built-in mic and a remote with a speaker
The overdue Apple TV refresh makes it easier to talk to Siri and find your remote.
The overdue Apple TV refresh makes it easier to talk to Siri and find your remote.
If you happen to misplace the remote, the new integrated speaker should make it easier to track down. It could play an audio alert to guide you to its location, whether it got carelessly kicked under the couch or a child mischievously hid it in a drawer.
This is on top of the upgrade to an A19 chip that will power Siri AI. The Apple TV is expected to start shipping on October 30th, alongside the refreshed HomePod Mini.

title_en: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
title_fa: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
excerpt_en: On Equity, we debate the impact of data center moratoriums and whether the AI industry has a communication problem.
excerpt_fa: On Equity, we debate the impact of data center moratoriums and whether the AI industry has a communication problem.
content_en:
Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities.
Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried.
Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication.
“We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular.
There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc.
I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point.
This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip.
The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too.
So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now.
Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years.
But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this.
Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.]
So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.”
But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.
It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step.
Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc.

Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities.
Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried.
Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication.
“We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular.
There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc.
I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point.
This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip.
The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too.
So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now.
Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years.

title_en: Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
title_fa: Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
excerpt_en: Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
excerpt_fa: Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
content_en:
Why strong magnets can hinder the iPhone's rear-facing camera
Magnetic accessories can be handy, but make sure they're not interfering with your camera.
Apple continues to up its camera game. This September, Apple debuted its iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, a lineup which introduced its most advanced camera system to date. The new 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera comes with variable aperture, low-light sensor and pro controls that render sharper shots for amateurs and professionals alike. But what if I told you that your phone's accessories could ruin these photos outright?
Frequently, your favorite iPhone accessory depends on strong magnets and magnetized metal plates to stick to your phone's casing. Whether you're using a removable grip, car mount, power bank or ring lights, you are potentially placing strong magnetic fields. And while they likely don't affect your phone's internal systems, Apple has found that these magnets interfere with your phone's camera.
This occurs because the rear-facing cameras on your iPhone use image stabilization technologies to prevent blurring and preserve focus. Such lens-position sensors are hypersensitive to magnetic fields and may become disabled when near certain accessories. On its support page, Apple suggests magnetic accessories may cause your camera's images to blur. Other auxiliary factors, such as exposure to high amplitude vibrations, such as those produced by high-powered motorcycles, can also cause lasting damage to these camera sensors.
All about the magnets
Your iPhone relies on two magnet-sensitive lens-positioning sensor technologies to stabilize your camera's pictures. The first is known as optical image stabilization, or OIS, which uses a gyroscope to sense the movements of your camera when taking a photo. If you move while taking a photo, your OIS will reduce how much the image blurs by adjusting the lens to match the gyroscope's movements. In doing so, OIS reduces image motion, allowing you to take sharp, crisp images.
The second, known as closed-loop autofocus, prevents gravity and vibrations from causing motion blur through onboard accelerometers, a form of magnetic sensor that measures these outside factors and compensates your camera's lens position. By adjusting its lenses' focus, your iPhone can preserve the sharpness in your videos, panoramas, and camera stills.
Magnets can have a pronounced effect on these photo-correction processes. This is because lens-position sensors are sensitive to the interference cause by strong magnetic fields. If you place a magnet too close to your camera lens, you may notice that its motion sensing becomes less accurate. The range of your camera's lens may also be limited. And while your camera's autofocus and OIS sensors may be disabled, your camera will still be able to take photos using other stabilization methods.
Luckily, the solution to this problem is simple: avoid accessories that place magnetic fields close to your cameras. In particular, Apple warns users to be wary of third-party accessories with strong magnets like latch folio covers or car mounts. When shopping for your next favorite iPhone accessory, consider whether worse picture quality may be an unfortunate tradeoff. Of course, avoiding magnets doesn't guarantee that your camera will work without a hitch, since there may be more underlying issues at work. For a step-by-step guide to troubleshooting your iPhone's camera, visit Apple's support page.

title_en: Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
title_fa: Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
excerpt_en: Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
excerpt_fa: Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
content_en:
Apple's smart home hub will reportedly be called HomeView
Bloomberg reported that the HomeView device will start shipping in November.
Just ahead of Apple's smart home event on Tuesday, we may finally have a name for the long-awaited smart home hub. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the device that will serve as a Siri command center for a user's Apple-powered smart home will be called the "HomeView" and will make its big debut during the company's "Welcome home" event.
The smart home hub is expected to pair with Apple's other smart home devices, like the HomePod mini that's also expected to get a refresh. However, Gurman explained that the "View" portion of the name is meant to convey that the device will be a display that is primarily controlled through Siri and voice commands, instead of something like "HomePad," which would imply a tablet experience.
According to Gurman, the HomeView will come in a countertop version with a metal speaker base in space gray, silver, starlight and pink color options, as well as a wall-mounted model that will only come in space gray and silver. Unlike Apple's other hardware, the HomeView will only support a limited selection of Apple apps and won't have access to the App Store, Gurman reported. Instead, Apple reportedly wants users to lean on third-party accessories that can connect to the HomeView device through Siri, Apple's Home app or its devices.
To achieve that, Apple has been working with LG to develop several smart home devices, including doorbells, thermostats, outdoor security cameras and more. Gurman also reported that Apple is working with Schneider Electric SE for smart home devices across the European market, but that all of these third-party products will be available under the "Apple Home Collection."
To go along with the reported HomeView hub, Apple is expected to reveal a revamped HomePod mini with the S10 chip and a new Apple TV set-top box with the A19 chip, Gurman said. While the new HomePod mini and Apple TV are expected to start shipping and be available in Apple stores on October 30, the HomeView will release a few weeks later in mid-November, according to Gurman. The third-party products from LG should release after that, with Gurman predicting they will ship later this year at the earliest.

title_en: Apple Home's new AI summaries for security cameras cost more than you'd think
title_fa: Apple Home's new AI summaries for security cameras cost more than you'd think
excerpt_en: If you have a lot of cameras in your home, get ready to pay for more expensive iCloud+ plans.
excerpt_fa: If you have a lot of cameras in your home, get ready to pay for more expensive iCloud+ plans.
content_en:
Apple Home's new AI summaries for security cameras cost more than you'd think
Get ready to pay for more expensive iCloud+ plans.
With the release of iOS 27, Apple is deploying its much-anticipated Siri AI suite of features across its software ecosystem. One noteworthy change is coming to Apple HomeKit, as the Cupertino company injects Apple Intelligence into its home security camera system.
The upgrade launches Apple's video summary feature, where you can generate descriptions of videos caught on your home security system. The feature groups together related clips across multiple cameras for a comprehensive picture of a specific event, allowing you to easily review events that occur at your home. For instance, Apple's press release announcing the feature shows a man identified as Robert arriving at a home with a fruit bowl of fruit, an example showcasing how HomeKit's Apple Intelligence and Face Recognition software work together to generate these summaries. You can also search these recordings using natural language queries, as well as group similar videos together to reduce notifications. And while your willingness to invite yet another AI algorithm into your life may vary, it's no doubt that the new feature is another sign of AI's continued push into modern smart homes.
Notably, the feature won't be available to all Apple HomeKit users. As it stands, you must have at least a 2nd generation HomePod, HomePod Mini or Apple TV 4K running Apple's latest operating system. You also need to use an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, nominally the iPhone 15 Pro or later. But the biggest barrier is likely the price of the program's cloud storage, which could cost you up to $60 per month, depending on your number of cameras. For a list of compatible cameras, visit Apple's Smart Home Accessory website.
A costly new feature
Charging extra for a HomeKit Secure video cloud storage plan isn't anything new. Prior to the AI update, users could hook up a network of cameras using 50 GB, 200 GB, and 2 TB iCloud+ plans. However, the new AI features require you to pay for significantly more expensive iCloud+ plans. For just a single camera, for instance, you will need to invest in Apple's 2 TB iCloud+ plan, which will add $9.99 to your expenses. This monthly bill scales as you grow your home smart camera network. To operate a second Apple Intelligence-enabled camera, you'll need to upgrade to Apple's $29.99/month, 6 TB plan. Anything between 3 and the maximum 5 camera setup necessitates 12 TB of iCloud storage. This means that operating Apple Intelligence-enabled cameras around your home could cost a whopping $59.99 a month, meaning you may add more than $700 to your yearly household costs. Notably, this cloud storage is in addition your family's iCloud storage plan.
Now, it's worth mentioning that you can enjoy the benefits of Apple Intelligence's HomeKit upgrades without deploying it across all your security cameras. For instance, you may want the AI summary feature for your front porch camera to track deliveries but may not find the same utility in analyzing the possum scurrying past your back window. Selectively deploying the feature may help reduce costs.
However, its just as important to note that these prices aren't necessarily static. In its Apple Intelligence support page, Apple notes that supported cameras and iCloud+ features "may change over time." Given the volatile pricing of AI-ladened subscriptions as companies desperately seek out profitability, it's wise to view the consistency of these price structures with a dose of skepticism. Luckily, the feature is optional, so you won't be registered into a costly subscription if you don't plan on utilizing the feature. For now, anyway.
Setting up HomeKit's AI features
If Apple's home surveillance AI summary tool seems worth the investment, you can set up your new AI-enabled security system directly in your iPhone, iPad, or Mac. First, make sure your HomeKit Secure Video system is set up on your iPhone or iPad by going to Settings > your name > iCloud > Show All, > Home. If using a Mac, go to the Apple menu > System Settings > Your name, located at the top of the sidebar. From there, click iCloud > See All, Show All, or Show More Apps > Home.
To enable Home camera video descriptions, go to your iPhone's Home app. Next, tap the Home tab, hit the three dotted icon and select Home Settings. Here, you can turn on Apple Intelligence. Once completed, you can choose which cameras you would like to enable or disable the video descriptions feature for.
If you want your HomeKit to recognize visitors from your camera roll, return to your iPhone's Home app. After adding your camera to your Home app's homepage, go to Recognize Familiar Faces, turn on Face Recognition, and tap Continue. To add recent visitors to your camera's catalog, go to the Home tab, tap the camera, and select the gear icon. Next, go to Face Recognition, tap the unidentified person in your Recent list, and tap Add Name. Here, you can add appropriate identifiers and even choose whether you'd like to be notified whenever said person enters your camera view.
To stop your smart home system from alerting you every time a racoon treks by, reduce your notifications through the Home app on your iPhone. Visit your system settings by going to Home > three dotted icon > Home Settings. Next, tap Apple Intelligence, and enable Reduce Notifications.

title_en: TechCrunch Mobility: A roadblock clears for self-driving trucks
title_fa: TechCrunch Mobility: A roadblock clears for self-driving trucks
excerpt_en: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
excerpt_fa: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
content_en:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
I’m back from a sojourn through New Hampshire’s White Mountains — a few days of respite before Disrupt 2026, TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco. Now, after a few days immersed in fall colors, I am ready for the action. And there is gonna be a lot of it.
I want to see you all there, so here is a 30% discount on tickets to Disrupt with code mobility30. For more info on the show, scroll down.
Now, on to the news!
Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization.
Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices.
It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.)
Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works.
Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.”
Gerardo Interiano, Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.”
One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry?
A little bird
It’s been a few months since Redwood Materials, the battery-recycling company started by Tesla co-founder JB Straubel, kicked off a restructuring to focus more on energy storage. The first stage of the restructuring involved laying off around 135 employees, or 10% of its workforce.
But a little bird recently told us that some more executives were on their way out the door. Sure enough, over the last few weeks, Redwood’s vice presidents of engineering, operations, treasury, and external affairs have all left the startup.
Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected] or my Signal at kkorosec.07, or email Sean O’Kane at [email protected].
Deals!
Waymo has relied on capital from its parent company Alphabet and high-profile venture firms to fund its autonomous vehicle tech plans. This week, the company turned to debt financing for the first time for another bump. A $5 billion bump to be exact.
PIMCO, Blackstone, and Sixth Street were the lead lenders. But there were so many more, including Capital Group, Loomis Sayles, T. Rowe Price, Apollo, Blue Owl, Diameter Capital Partners, Franklin Templeton, Fidelity Management & Research Company, HPS Investment Partners, and Oaktree.
The debt financing comes as the company accelerates its commercial expansion within existing cities while pushing into new markets in the United States, Europe, and Japan.
Other deals that got my attention this week …
Bloom has raised $3.6 million to become the “Alibaba” of American manufacturing. The seed round was led by SNAK Venture Partners and included Flyover Capital, deep tech firm Mana Ventures, Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.
Flai, a startup that developed AI software for dealerships, raised $27 million in a Series A funding round led by automation-focused firm Base10 Partners. The round included funding from dealers (Friedkin Group and Findlay Automotive), Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator, and First Round Capital.
Parallel Systems, a startup developing a rail vehicle capable of moving over several tons of freight as far as 500 miles without an operator, raised $100 million in a Series C round led by AVP, with participation from Hillspire, Agility Global, Cobalt Capital, Anthos Capital, Congruent Ventures, Riot Ventures, and Collaborative Fund.
Uber has agreed to buy catering company ezCater in an all-cash transaction valued at $2.3 billion.

I’m back from a sojourn through New Hampshire’s White Mountains — a few days of respite before Disrupt 2026, TechCrunch’s annual tech conference in San Francisco. Now, after a few days immersed in fall colors, I am ready for the action. And there is gonna be a lot of it.

Now, on to the news!
Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization.
Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. title_en: Dawn Myers is making it easier to style, detangle, and care for curly hair
title_fa: Dawn Myers is making it easier to style, detangle, and care for curly hair
excerpt_en: Richualist is one of TechCrunch's Battlefield 200 Companies!
excerpt_fa: Richualist is one of TechCrunch's Battlefield 200 Companies!
content_en:
Normally, Dawn Myers wears her hair up in a big old afro, and anyone with an afro can attest that wash days — the routine of washing and styling textured hair — are often tedious. They take a lot of detangling, product, styling, and, well, time.
“I was watching ‘Shark Tank,’ and there was another curly girl idea,” she recalled of a day around eight years ago, when a pitch for a hair product aired. She started thinking about all the hair tools on the market, like blow dryers and curling irons, “things that straighten and change the chemistry of our naturally curly hair,” she told TechCrunch, adding that it takes around an hour and 20 minutes to wash and style her own hair.
None of those tools help with that, and for Myers, it highlighted a gap that has always existed in the beauty hardware space — a lack of tooling for textured hair. It’s a space that’s complex, expensive, and just overlooked.
“If you think back to slavery, we were mandated to cover our hair. That’s where do-rags come from. You had to cover your hair. Why? Because our hair was seen as ugly and unkempt and unacceptable,” she said. Later came hot combs, chemical relaxers, and flat irons, all of which straighten textured hair. “It’s only been the past 15 years or so where women of color and Black women in particular and, quite frankly, white women as well have really felt comfortable exposing their naturally curly hair and really just embracing it.”
Soon after that episode aired, she whipped out a legal pad and sketched out a business idea, then went to Ace Hardware and CVS and put together a “Frankenstein-looking prototype.”
Her idea eventually became the company Richualist, which is known for its product Mint, a hair tool that helps detangle, condition, gel, and style in a single stroke using refillable product pods. It even has warming technology to gently heat the product before it’s applied.
“We get that styling time down to about seven to 10 minutes,” she said. “It’s a massive game changer for the customer really stressed out by wash day.” She said her product, which also comes in travel size, helps make hair a bit healthier, reducing shedding and breakage by up to 70% since people no longer need to tug endlessly on their strands as they wash and style.
She built it with the materials science company Dow, after an early prototype caught the company’s attention during a startup accelerator program. “It just so happens that Dow had identified this white space recently as well, and they were starting a textured hair care unit,” she said. “So they ended up collaborating with us and giving us a lot of engineering help and manufacturing guidance.”
Even though she eventually became one of the first 100 Black women to raise more than $1 million in venture funding, the early days were rough. “It’s really impossible to get hardware funded,” she continued. “It’s even more impossible to get it funded when we’re talking about such a niche problem.”
She recalled the early meetings with executives in the beauty industry. “There are no people who look like me in those R&D suites.” In fact, she said, when she described wash days, “these people didn’t know what a wash day was. They didn’t understand that there’s this whole process that their customers have to go through.” She would tell them how painful and arduous the process is. “And the powers that be, up until this point, did not know,” she continued. “Even the bonds in our hair are totally different than other technology types. We really do need bespoke technology.”
Myers sold her home and liquidated her 401(k) retirement account to fund the initial development of this product. “That was a crazy bet, but it paid off,” she said. “We were able to get about $1.4 million in the door to commercialize the product and just validate it.” Overall, it took about five years of development to get the product to “a place where it made sense to the customer,” she said, adding that her team also had to conduct their own research in the space since what they needed — like how much product the average person with textured hair uses — didn’t yet exist.
Then, in 2022, just as she was about to expand and go to market, she was diagnosed with stage three colorectal cancer. “We ended up closing our round while I was still going through treatment,” she recalled, saying the round took “forever” to close. She remembers sitting in the chemo chair at Johns Hopkins, on her laptop, trying to close deals. She applied to Shark Tank in 2023 and appeared on the show later that year, though the episode aired in 2024. “I was still wearing a binder around my abdomen [a compression wrap] under the dress I wore for my ‘Shark Tank’ experience,” she said.
She ended up nabbing a deal from investor Mark Cuban and serial entrepreneur Emma Grede, which helped her formally launch the product. Grede then helped it expand into Ulta’s online website earlier this year.
“We’re actually about to market ourselves as sold out,” she said, adding that the company is mapping out ways to expand further.
Her company was picked as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 startups this year, earning a spot at TechCrunch Disrupt, the publication’s annual startup conference, which kicks off this Tuesday.
When asked how she first heard about Disrupt, she laughed. “I mean, who doesn’t know about Disrupt?” She said she’s bracing herself, as an introvert, for all the people she will meet and conversations she will have.
“But what I am most excited for is textured hair to be sitting on the stage with some of the most sophisticated tech in the space.”

title_en: Here's how long your Google Pixel phone will get software updates
title_fa: Here's how long your Google Pixel phone will get software updates
excerpt_en: Your Google Pixel phone has a set lifetime of support based on when it first went on sale. After that, you have few options for using it securely.
excerpt_fa: Your Google Pixel phone has a set lifetime of support based on when it first went on sale. After that, you have few options for using it securely.
content_en:
Here's how long your Google Pixel phone will get software updates
Google offers great support for Pixels, but not all models enjoy the full timeline.
With the release of the Pixel 8 in 2023, Google made a widely celebrated announcement. Going forward, Pixel phones would receive seven years of software updates — not only routine security patches but major OS upgrades, too. It was a more robust promise than even Samsung, the largest vendor of Android devices, had made in 2019 when it pledged three years of major OS updates for lower-end Galaxy devices and seven for select flagships. A quick loss of software support had previously been a major reason why Android phones failed to hold their value for long, so committing to that support was crucial for the future.
A lot of popular smartphones are in their last year of support right now, but how many years of life does your Pixel phone have left? That may not be obvious unless you know the exact month and year it hit the market. Google begins the window of service for a given Pixel smartphone in the month it became available for purchase on the Google Store website in the US.
Newer Pixel phones get five to seven years of software updates
Google's Pixel release date page is a helpful guide here. First, all Pixels from the original model through the Pixel 5a are obsolete and no longer receiving updates.
If you have a phone in the Pixel 6 or 7 families, or the original Pixel Fold, it will receive updates for five years from the month it went on sale. That means the Pixel 7 and 7 Pro will get their final update by the end of October 2027, while the Pixel 6 and 6 Pro are currently reaching their end of support in October 2026. Pixel a-series phones are released on a different cadence, so support windows differ accordingly. The Pixel 7a will cease updates after May 2028, while the Pixel 6a will lose support after July 2027.
The Pixel 8 and later are guaranteed to get seven years of support, meaning the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro will stop receiving updates after October 2030. It's thus still worth picking up a discounted Pixel 8 with the life it has in it. The Pixel 9 and 9 Pro (released in August-September 2024) will do the same after those months in 2031, the 2025 Pixel 10 and 10 Pro after August 2032, and the new Pixel 11 and 11 Pro after August 2033.
The Pixel 8a, released in May 2024, will see support expire after May 2031. The Pixel 9a, which shipped in April 2025 after a March announcement, will receive no further updates after April 2032. Lastly, the Pixel 10a, which released slightly less than a year later, will receive a final update around March 2033.
Your options are limited once updates stop on a Pixel phone
If you want to keep your Pixel phone alive after Google kicks it off the update schedule, you have few options. Of course, you can keep using it with the last software update it receives, but this will expose your phone to security risks in the long run. Part of an Android phone's routine update schedule includes security patches, generally issued on a monthly cadence. Once those updates stop, new security issues that get discovered won't be fixed, leaving owners of older devices exposed. You should get a new phone if possible, or at least upgrade to one that still receives security updates.
You might assume that installing a custom ROM or OS image onto your old Pixel would give it new life after Google abandons it. However, whether you go for a full-scale OS with a locked bootloader like the privacy-focused GrapheneOS, or opt for a ROM with an unlocked bootloader like LineageOS, you won't be fully protected from security threats. That's not to say you can't run DIY software on an out-of-service Pixel, but rather that any updates pushed to those projects will not benefit from original equipment manufacturer (OEM) firmware, kernel and vendor code. See GrapheneOS's explanation if you're curious.
If hardened security isn't important to you, LineageOS is the most well-supported ROM. It runs on an unlocked bootloader, so apps that demand stringent security on a verified boot such as banking, mobile wallets and games with anti-cheat measures will no longer work. However, Lineage is still supporting the original Pixel from 2016, along with nearly every other Pixel phone since. On a deprecated Pixel, you'll receive LineageOS security patches for the Linux kernel and framework security, covering some but far from all of your bases.

content_en:
If you thought you’d seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission, you’re wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
NASA’s treasure trove of images, audio, and video offers an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
NASA’s treasure trove of images, audio, and video offers an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes. Impact flashes have been seen before, but these ones on the dark side of the Moon could have been the faintest observed with the human eye, and everyone’s excitement is palpable in the clip.
Alongside the dump, NASA also released a trio of documents that help supplement the trove of unfiltered data. That includes the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

excerpt_en: George A. Romero is obviously best known as the father of the modern zombie movie. But between inventing the genre with Night of the Living Dead and his outbreak horror, The Crazies, Romero made two much lesser-known films: There's Always Vanilla, which I'll admit I've never...

content_en:
George A. Romero is obviously best known as the father of the modern zombie movie. But between inventing the genre with Night of the Living Dead and his outbreak horror, The Crazies, Romero made two much lesser-known films: There’s Always Vanilla, which I’ll admit I’ve never seen, and Season of the Witch, or, as it was originally titled, Hungry Wives.
George A. Romero’s Season of the Witch is a slow-burn feminist occult drama
After inventing the modern zombie, Romero made a feminist film about a suffering house wife turning to witchcraft.
After inventing the modern zombie, Romero made a feminist film about a suffering house wife turning to witchcraft.
Hungry Wives was supposed to be an exploitation film. The studio marketed it as a softcore porn, but it failed to find an audience — probably because the movie features minimal nudity, just one sex scene, and lots of talking. It was an undeniable flop upon its release in 1973. It was eventually rereleased as Season of the Witch after Romero’s Dawn of the Dead sparked renewed interest in his work.
While sadly, Romero’s original 130-minute cut of the film has been lost, parts of it have been recovered and restored, expanding the 89-minute original release to 104 minutes. An obvious reason for its failure, beyond the distributor butchering it by cutting 40 minutes, is that what Romero made wasn’t softcore porn; instead, it’s a slow-burn feminist drama where the occult is almost incidental.
Protagonist Joan Mitchell is trapped in an abusive marriage and unhappy with her role as a submissive housewife. She eventually turns to therapy, then to witchcraft, in an attempt to escape her humdrum life.
Season of the Witch has its issues, for sure. The production value is quite low — apparently the movie was made for just $100,000 (around $800,000 adjusted for inflation). The acting is also wildly uneven. While star Jan White turns in an excellent performance, others appear to be reading off cue cards or chew scenery with Pacino-levels of camp.
Still, there’s something compelling about Romero’s directing and his, for the time, boldly progressive take on feminism. For all of its reliance on dialogue over action, Season of the Witch still manages a tense and, at times, hallucinatory atmosphere. And it all leads to a somewhat predictable, but still extremely satisfying ending.

But between inventing the genre with Night of the Living Dead and his outbreak horror, The Crazies, Romero made two much lesser-known films: There’s Always Vanilla, which I’ll admit I’ve never seen, and Season of the Witch, or, as it was originally titled, Hungry Wives.
George A. Romero’s Season of the Witch is a slow-burn feminist occult drama
After inventing the modern zombie, Romero made a feminist film about a suffering house wife turning to witchcraft.
After inventing the modern zombie, Romero made a feminist film about a suffering house wife turning to witchcraft.
Hungry Wives was supposed to be an exploitation film. The studio marketed it as a softcore porn, but it failed to find an audience — probably because the movie features minimal nudity, just one sex scene, and lots of talking. It was an undeniable flop upon its release in 1973. It was eventually rereleased as Season of the Witch after Romero’s Dawn of the Dead sparked renewed interest in his work.

title_en: The hidden features every Waze user should know about
title_fa: The hidden features every Waze user should know about
excerpt_en: There are a load of features tucked away in Google's 'other' mapping app.
excerpt_fa: There are a load of features tucked away in Google's 'other' mapping app.
content_en:
The hidden features every Waze user should know about
There are a load of features tucked away in Google's 'other' mapping app.
There are some services that become most people's default simply by doing many things right, and Google Maps is one of them. Its coverage across different countries and reliable navigation make it difficult to replace. Apple Maps has long since recoverd from its disastrous launch, but most people looking for an alternative will tend to gravitate toward Waze — which Google has owned since 2013. The app still looks and feels a lot different from Google Maps, though, with a stronger emphasis on the real-time driving experience.
Since Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app, it relies on real road users to report things like accidents, potholes, traffic congestion and police activity as they encounter them. Beyond navigation, Waze offers a surprisingly useful set of features that many users may not be aware of, since these options are often buried inside the app's menus. For starters, if you're traveling to a friend's place and you have their address saved on your phone, Waze makes it easier to start navigating there without having to manually enter the address every time.
Open Waze, swipe up and scroll to the very bottom where it says "Drive to friends & family." You'll need to grant Waze access to your contacts for this feature to work. Once enabled, simply type your friend or family member's name in the search box. As long as you have an address saved for that contact, Waze will let you begin navigation with a tap.
It's understandable if you're uncomfortable sharing your entire contacts list with Waze. If you want to revoke this permission, navigate to Settings > Apps > Waze > Contacts and tap on None on an iPhone. For Android, head to Settings > Apps > See all apps > Waze > Permissions > Contacts and tap on "Don't Allow."
Use your own voice for directions
Waze is already known for being more customizable than its competitors. For instance, you can select a "Mood" by navigating to Settings > View profile > Mood. This lets you pick how your avatar shows up for other Waze users, so if you're in a particularly bad mood, you can pick an avatar that matches your energy. You can also select a sidekick, which adds a little bit of personality to the navigation experience by changing your vehicle's icon, avatar and even the voice that guides you along your route.
What's even cooler is that Waze lets you record instructions in your own voice. You can, of course, have a friend or family member do the voice lines for you. A TikTok user shared how they used this Waze feature to capture their kid's adorable voice to make every drive a little more special. You can change voice packs on Waze by heading to Settings > Voice and sound > Current voice. There is a vast selection of presets you can choose from, or you can tap "New voice" to record your own set of navigation prompts.
Waze lists a total of 39 (yes, I counted) different prompts for you to record, with a maximum recording length of six seconds. There are voice lines for everything from basic turn instructions to warnings about hazards and speed cameras. If you don't record a phrase in your own voice, Waze will play the default navigation voice for that instruction instead. Although, if you don't want to be caught off guard when a completely different voice suddenly chimes in, it might be worth recording all 39 prompts.
Plan a drive with Waze
Another useful Waze feature that often goes underutilized is the ability to plan your trips ahead of time. If there's a commute you need to make later in the day or an appointment you have scheduled for another date, Waze can recommend when you should leave based on the expected traffic along the route. There are two ways to schedule trips using Waze. The easiest is to search for your destination as usual and tap on the "Leave later" button instead of "Go now."
This will let you pick your arrival time in increments of 15 minutes. Waze also displays the expected traffic levels next to the selected arrival time. You can change your starting location as well as the day of the week if you want to schedule a drive further in advance. Tapping on "Save" will add the trip to your planned drives. You can view this list by tapping on the hamburger menu and heading to "Plan a drive." Here, Waze also lets you connect your calendar so any upcoming events that have a location attached can automatically show up as planned drives.
If you want to dig even deeper into Waze, there's another hidden trick worth exploring — secret codes that can be entered into the search bar. They let you access a couple of the app's diagnostic tools and toggle certain features. For instance, entering "##@morph" unlocks a secret monster mood avatar for your profile and "##@cctts" clears the app's text-to-speech cache, which can fix certain issues you're having with voice navigation. There are other Waze search codes you can try, but it's best not to mess with ones that are intended for troubleshooting.

title_en: Efferon wants to eradicate the devastating toll of pediatric sepsis
title_fa: Efferon wants to eradicate the devastating toll of pediatric sepsis
excerpt_en: This Battlefield 200 startup has developed blood-purification tech to save children
excerpt_fa: This Battlefield 200 startup has developed blood-purification tech to save children
content_en:
Sepsis, an acute inflammation triggered by infection, is a leading cause of childhood mortality, claiming roughly 3 million children under the age of five annually.
Efferon, a startup selected as one of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s Startup Battlefield 200, is on a mission to drastically lower that number.
The company has developed a medical device that it says lowers organ failure rates and significantly accelerates recovery in children.
When standard treatments like antibiotics cannot stop the immune system’s overreaction, a patient’s blood must be filtered to remove deadly toxins. That is where Efferon’s devices, of absorbers of dangerous cytokines and toxins, step in to make a critical difference.
Dima Romashin, Efferon’s co-founder and CEO, compares what happens in the body during sepsis to a fire, where an immune response overwhelms the body rapidly. “In a fire, there are two things: the flame itself and smoke that it produces,” he told TechCrunch.
In sepsis, endotoxins are the flames and cytokines are the smoke. Efferon, unlike other devices on the market, has developed a mechanism that can absorb both at once, according to Romashin.
Although Efferon makes absorbers for adults, Efferon NEO, its pediatric device developed specifically for young kids, is proving especially effective. Since children have a significantly lower circulating blood volume, they require medical devices engineered specifically for their physiology, according to Romashin.
In April, Efferon NEO received a CE mark, Europe’s equivalent to FDA approval, making it the first multimodal blood purification device specifically engineered for pediatric sepsis.
Efferon NEO is used in intensive care units across 30 countries, including European hospitals, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand. The company is now preparing to file for FDA approval and is on track to hit $2 million in annualized revenue by the end of 2026.
The startup’s technology was originally developed by scientists at Moscow State University, including co-founder Ivan Bessonov. Recognizing its potential, Romashin, a serial entrepreneur, stepped in earlier this year as CEO to help commercialize it.
Although Romashin admits that Efferon isn’t growing at the breakneck pace of today’s AI startups, true success for the company is measured by something else entirely: every child who gets to go home.

title_en: We're in the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage and GTA 6 will only make it worse
title_fa: We're in the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage and GTA 6 will only make it worse
excerpt_en: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to become the most popular game ever and Sony is finding it very difficult to satisfy demand for the PlayStation 5 Pro.
excerpt_fa: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to become the most popular game ever and Sony is finding it very difficult to satisfy demand for the PlayStation 5 Pro.
content_en:
We're in the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage and GTA 6 will only make it worse
More power, improved visuals and no PC release are ramping demand.
Sony has a PS5 Pro problem. As fans clamor for the gaming console ahead of the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the Japanese company will likely struggle to meet global demand until at least 2027. According to an exclusive report by German gaming outlet Playfront, Sony has told distribution partners that "temporary market supply constraints and high demand" will continue to limit retailer's stock of consoles until next year.
First released in November 2024, the PS5 Pro arrived with an upgraded GPU, heightened graphics at 60 fps performance, advanced ray tracing, 2TB of memory and AI-driven upscaling to deliver sharper images. Despite being nearly two years old, however, supply constraints and soaring demand continue to push the console's cost into the stratosphere, with MSRP prices now $200 above its initial $699.99 asking price.
With store supplies dwindling and limited restocks, opportunists are making a fortune on the resale market, pricing the console hundreds of dollars above its already-elevated market price. At Best Buy, for instance, one reseller priced their PlayStation 5 Pro console at a jaw dropping $1,539.
It won't get any better with the upcoming release of GTA 6. Set to launch on November 19, fans are eager to end the 13 year-drought between installments of the popular franchise. Offering an expansive world and incredible graphics, it's understandable that consumers want to maximize their playing experience by purchasing the latest console. But will consumers be able to get their hands on the PS5 Pro in time for the November launch? And will the game prove worthy of splurging on a new console?
Inside the PS5 Pro bottleneck
PlayStation supply chain issues are nothing new. In 2020, global chip shortages constrained Sony's PS5 output for over three years, with customers often waiting months before receiving the latest console. This time around, the AI boom has limited consumer tech manufacturers' access to advanced chips, creating supply bottlenecks and price hikes across the industry. And although companies have invested more than $770 billion over the past half decade in American semiconductor production alone, it may take years before supplies rebound given current demand.
To Sony's credit, the PlayStation 5 Pro isn't the only piece of hardware suffering supply constraints. According to a report by The Economist, laptop prices have increased by 20 percent this year, as companies like Apple and Microsoft raise prices to offset component development costs and AI hardware investments. In South Korea, factory-gate prices for DRAM and flash memory have skyrocketed by 445 percent and 244 percent, respectively, due in large part to AI-driven scarcity.
In the meantime, Sony may have to get creative in how it delivers the high-end console to its customers. In Japan, for instance, Sony has instituted a lottery system for gamers looking to snag its most advanced console, adding conditions like minimum gaming times to weed out opportunists looking to make a quick buck on the resale market. If supplies continue to lag behind demand, such precautions may become a necessity.
Do you need a PS5 Pro for GTA 6?
It is easy to see why gamers are rushing for new consoles. Extended previews of Rockstar's upcoming megahit showcased a phantasmagoria of gritty realism, with hyper-realistic visuals and the franchise's most expansive gameplay yet.
Following the gameplay trailers and deep dives, gamers scurried to snag their new consoles in hopes of maximizing the game's anticipated visuals and improved performance. Much like IMAX productions grip moviegoers, the Pro will likely squeeze the most out of the Rockstar's hotly-anticipated title. With no PC port release date in sight, consumers are somewhat forced to grab the most advanced PlayStation console.
Ironically, it's unclear whether GTA 6 will be capable of maximizing the PS5 Pro's most advanced features. Although marketed as PS5 Pro Enhanced, a label PlayStation uses for games with "improved visuals and performance," neither Sony or Rockstar have stated how the game will be meaningfully different on the console. For example, earlier this summer, rumors circulated that the game would support 60 fps on the PS5 Pro. However, experts remain skeptical, as Rockstar executives continue to state that the game would run on 30 fps on both consoles. For what it's worth, footage from Rockstar's official previews of the game have been played on a PlayStation 5 at 30 fps.
Some skeptics maintain that Grand Theft Auto 6 likely won't be able to maintain high framerates on the PS5 Pro due to its scale. The PS5 Pro's 10 percent CPU gains may help the game better render crowds and traffic, but likely won't increase its performance in other areas.
More than likely, gamers will still benefit from the PS5 Pro's enhanced visual effects. One example may be the PS5 Pro's leaps in ray tracing, which produce more realistic light and reflections. However, with Sony bringing the PS5 Pro's QSSR AI upscaling to its base model, the gap between the two consoles may be quite narrow.
