title_en: How to lock apps on your Samsung Galaxy phone
title_fa: How to lock apps on your Samsung Galaxy phone
excerpt_en: Samsung phones have a couple of features that can keep sensitive apps and files private. One locks your chosen apps, and the other restricts all but one app.
excerpt_fa: Samsung phones have a couple of features that can keep sensitive apps and files private. One locks your chosen apps, and the other restricts all but one app.
content_en:
How to lock apps on your Samsung Galaxy phone
Keep your kid from ordering a five-pound bag of candy.
Handing your phone to your kid for a few minutes of game time shouldn't mean they end up three menus deep in your banking apps, emails or texts. That's a common enough worry that plenty of Galaxy owners go searching for a simple way to lock their apps, much like iPhone users can do. Well, Samsung doesn't offer one.
On an iPhone, the fix is a quick long-press and selecting Require Face ID. The app then won't open without a face or fingerprint scan. Samsung takes a different approach to this whole situation. Instead of a single toggle, Galaxy phones split the job between two tools: Secure Folder and app pinning. Neither one is a direct copy of Apple's version, but together they cover more ground. At the end of the day, the important part is that you'll be able to keep prying eyes away from apps they shouldn't have access to.
Why Samsung skipped the simple app lock
Samsung phased out a basic app lock option in favor of Secure Folder, a more robust system built on Samsung Knox, the company's security platform. Rather than just gating an app behind a password, Secure Folder creates an entirely separate, encrypted space on the phone. Apps placed there run as isolated copies, with their own data and sign-ins kept apart from the rest of the device.
That's quite the difference from how Apple does things since iOS locks an app in place, while Secure Folder essentially duplicates it inside a vault. The trade-off is setup time, because Secure Folder takes quite a few extra steps. Given the complexity of the task, there's been quite a bit of pushback over the years as users argued a lighter-weight lock would suit everyday needs like keeping kids out of TikTok. For quick, temporary restrictions, Samsung offers a second option called app pinning. This one works more like a makeshift version of Apple's screen-lock tools.
How to lock apps using Secure Folder
If you want to keep sensitive information safe on your phone, Secure Folder is the way to go. This won't just protect your data from your kids, but also from thieves and nosy relatives. It's the best place to put your banking apps, messaging tools, private photos and anything else worth encrypting. Here's how to set it up:
-
Open Settings > Security and privacy > More security settings > Secure Folder.
-
Sign in with your Samsung Account.
-
Choose a lock type: PIN, password, pattern or biometric scan.
-
Choose whether the apps can still run in the background when the Secure Folder is closed.
-
Tap the plus icon inside Secure Folder and select the apps you want to add.
Apps moved there will be inaccessible until you unlock Secure Folder using your authentication method of choice. The best part is that you can hide the folder icon from the home screen for extra discretion, which you can do from the quick panel by turning off the Secure Folder app. The apps in Secure Folder won't continue to work in the background or create notifications when the folder is hidden, so be sure to unhide it when you're ready to use the apps therein. Just another something extra to consider when you're customizing your Samsung Galaxy phone.
How to use app pinning for quick restrictions
For all those situations where full encryption isn't called for, like letting a kid play one game without slipping into the Play Store to install some random app, app pinning gets the job done faster. So, before you hand your phone over, here's what you have to do:
-
Go to Settings > Security and privacy > More security settings and turn on Allow apps to be pinned.
-
Tap on the Recents button (the three vertical bars at the bottom of the screen) or, if you use swipe gestures, swipe up from the bottom of the screen and hold.
- Tap on the icon above the app you want to pin and select Pin this app or Pin to screen.
-
To unpin the app, you have to hold the Recents and Back buttons at the same time.
-
So, if you're letting your kid use your phone for one specific game, just open their game and pin the app. They won't be able to switch to a different app. Pinning doesn't encrypt anything, so it's not the right pick for financial or private apps, but it works just fine as a fast and temporary lockdown. Truth be told, this one will work best if your kids don't know how to read yet because you get on-screen directions on how to unpin the app when you tap on the bottom buttons.
For sensitive apps that need real protection, Secure Folder's Knox-backed encryption is the stronger option, even if it takes a few minutes to set up. For quick and low-stakes restrictions, like keeping a toddler inside a single game, app pinning gets the job done with almost no setup at all.

title_en: What is the 3-2-1 rule for backing up your data?
title_fa: What is the 3-2-1 rule for backing up your data?
excerpt_en: Make sure your files are safe in the event of a hard drive disaster.
excerpt_fa: Make sure your files are safe in the event of a hard drive disaster.
content_en:
What is the 3-2-1 rule for backing up your data?
Make sure your files are safe in the event of a hard drive disaster.
Whether it's photos, videos, financial records or an assortment of questionable personal poetry, you've probably generated stacks upon stacks of data over the years, figuratively speaking. While taking the time to make sure all that data is safe and backed up might not be your idea of an action-packed afternoon, there's a distinct and unpleasant panic that comes from realizing that your important files are gone for good. After all, no one wants to lose all those treasured cat photos. Fortunately, one fried hard drive doesn't have to leave you breathing into a paper bag and bargaining with the gods.
While there are different approaches out there to backing up your data, there's a classic rule you can use to get started. The 3-2-1 rule is a framework that covers how many copies of your data you need across how many types of media, and where that media should live. That way, if something happens to one of your copies, you have others you can rely on, keeping the panic at bay.
What is the 3-2-1 rule?
The 3-2-1 rule was first popularized by photographer Peter Krogh in his 2009 book, "The DAM Book: Digital Asset Management for Photographers." At a baseline, the rule says that you need three copies of your data stored on two types of media (often interpreted as two different devices in recent times), and that one of those should be kept offsite. Think about it like this: if you only have one copy of your favorite vacation photos stored on an SSD and something happens to that SSD, you're out of luck. Even if you take the steps to make copies to multiple drives, you could still lose everything in the event of a disaster like a flood, house fire or burglary. But if one of your copies lives somewhere else, you have another layer of protection. And ideally, that offsite copy would be located far enough away that the type of disaster that might affect your home wouldn't also affect the location of that other copy. In short, the rule emphasizes the importance of redundancies.
How to use the 3-2-1 rule
Over the years, the 3-2-1 rule has evolved as both tech and the threats against it have changed. Odds are you're not burning too many CDs these days. Plus, people tend to be a little less worried about media becoming obsolete. It's easy to find conversations in spots like Reddit showing how conscientious folks are interpreting the 3-2-1 rule to fit their needs, as well as what's feasible for them. Your data protection requirements won't be the same as a multinational corporation.
For example, you might have files on your laptop, an external hard drive and a private cloud server. You might also use a service like iCloud or Google Cloud, though it should be noted that depending on the service and syncing settings, deleting a file from your computer might also delete it from the cloud. There are also other services that offer automatic full backups of your devices, with various storage limitations and at various pricing tiers.
Additionally, there are more recent developments that have changed how the 3-2-1 rule gets interpreted and used, like the ever-shifting cybersecurity landscape. For one, an offsite copy can still be vulnerable to a ransomware attack if the device is networked.
Though the prospect of backing up your data might seem like a bear, the 3-2-1 rule can be a relatively straightforward way to think about preserving your important files. Taking a few steps to make copies and keeping those copies in different spots could be the difference between a full-blown crisis and the reassurance that all those cat pics, tax documents and even your finely-crafted haikus are safe.

Taking a few steps to make copies and keeping those copies in different spots could be the difference between a full-blown crisis and the reassurance that all those cat pics, tax documents and even your finely-crafted haikus are safe.

content_en:
In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft’s CEO laid out his views on the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models and how to confront those risks. Nadella says we can no longer accept a world where AI is treated as a “set of nested black boxes” whose advice and actions we simply accept or reject. He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leaves behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.”
Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are ‘compromised’
Microsoft’s CEO calls for putting an ‘emergency brake’ on AI.
Microsoft’s CEO calls for putting an ‘emergency brake’ on AI.
Many of his recommendations align with what we’ve heard from others in the industry: timely incident disclosure, independent audits, verifiable data, and containment. It’s on that last point that he appears to go slightly farther than some others in the field, saying:
We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on.
Unfortunately, Nadella also refers to AI as “super intelligence” throughout the post.

title_en: How does using your MacBook while charging affect its battery life?
title_fa: How does using your MacBook while charging affect its battery life?
excerpt_en: Modern MacBooks are pretty smart about managing their battery's health.
excerpt_fa: Modern MacBooks are pretty smart about managing their battery's health.
content_en:
How does using your MacBook while charging affect its battery life?
Modern MacBooks are pretty smart about managing their battery's health.
When you are deep in the zone, typing away on your MacBook, the last thing you want is for its battery to die in the middle of a work session. But is it safe to keep your device plugged in nonstop? There is a widely-held conception that doing so may fry your battery, or at least reduce its effectiveness. But in fact, thanks to the lithium batteries and smart charging software installed in new MacBooks, it's generally fine to keep your laptop plugged in at all times.
Still, there are some caveats, including accounting for unusual home electricity related issues like storms or blackouts, or overheating due to other factors. And there are some tricks to keeping your battery healthy that may include the occasional unplug, as well as a number of settings that promote battery health. Read on to learn tips for consistently charging your MacBook without impacting its battery life long-term.
Is it better to use a MacBook on battery or plugged in?
The short answer is that it typically doesn't make a difference. Mac computers use default software to monitor battery life and adjust to user habits and device power fluctuations. These tools work by monitoring its temperature history and charging patterns and modify charging accordingly. MacBooks (and basically all other laptops) run on lithium batteries, which have a high number of charge cycles. They also contain software that uses charging data to calculate when to reduce your battery's maximum charge, reducing wear and giving it more longevity.
The battery health management feature is activated by default on Mac laptops running on operating systems Catalina 10.15.5 (released in 2019) or later. If for some reason you've turned it off, you can activate it by going to your Apple menu, clicking "System Settings," and finding "Battery" in that sidebar. Click on "Battery Health" in this section and select "manage battery longevity."
While in the past, it was wise to avoid letting your battery charge to 100 percent and letting it stay there, today it's perfectly OK to keep your MacBook plugged in while using it. That's because the system will simply pause its charging cycle at optimized times.
How to protect your laptop's battery health over time
If you're worried about your MacBook's battery health, you can start by checking its status under "System Settings." Click "Battery" on the left-hand sidebar, and look at "Battery Health" to see its status – it will typically read "normal" or "service recommended." Some fluctuation is to be expected over time, but Apple doesn't recommend replacement until it passes below 80 percent capacity.
One instance in which battery levels are important to monitor is when storing your device long term: According to Apple, the best way to preserve battery health if not using your device for an extended period is to charge it to around 50 percent. "If you store it fully charged for an extended period of time, the battery may lose some capacity, leading to shorter battery life," its guide says.
The biggest issue affecting battery health is heat: If you're working outside at a cafe on a warm day, for example, you may want to unplug your device or move to a shadier spot. A computer heating up and charging at the same time could negatively impact battery health, and Apple lists MacBook Air operating temperature ranges as 50° to 95° F. In addition to warm environments, some cases or laptop stands can cause a device to overheat while charging. If you notice your device is getting hot, check to make sure its fans are unblocked. As a general rule, keeping batteries cool is one of the easiest ways to help them last longer.

title_en: Microsoft’s Satya Nadella says AI models need an ‘emergency brake’
title_fa: Microsoft’s Satya Nadella says AI models need an ‘emergency brake’
excerpt_en: In a Saturday morning post, Microsoft's CEO wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI.
excerpt_fa: In a Saturday morning post, Microsoft's CEO wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI.
content_en:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is the latest tech executive to offer lengthy thoughts on how AI safety might be improved.
In a Saturday morning post on X, Nadella wrote that it’s time “to step back and assess the trust architecture” of AI.
“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” Nadella wrote, using the Trump administration’s preferred term for AI.
As outlined by Nadella, this approach “means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” as well as “externalizing controls and safeguards.” He also called for “every meaningful model action” to be documented with “tamper-proof human readable evidence,” and for systems where “an authorized person” always has the ability “to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”
“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” he said. “Think of it like an emergency brake.”
Nadella’s comments come as leading AI companies acknowledge more and more incidents where they seemed to lose control of their models, and after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a plan for more cautious AI development.

title_en: Apple discloses deal to hire team and license tech from personalized podcast startup Huxe
title_fa: Apple discloses deal to hire team and license tech from personalized podcast startup Huxe
excerpt_en: Is Apple hoping to get into the AI-generated podcast business?
excerpt_fa: Is Apple hoping to get into the AI-generated podcast business?
content_en:
Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal.
As first reported in MacRumors, Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.”
Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.”)
In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down, with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data.
“The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.”
On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal.
The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans.
Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own, so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree.

title_en: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
title_fa: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
excerpt_en: Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that...
excerpt_fa: Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that...
content_en:
Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however.
DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.
Artists are frustrated with the lack of transparency around DistroKid removing their songs.
Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.
DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed.
Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track.
Music producer and marketing pro Jesse Cannon told The Verge that, “DistroKid gave up on customer service about two years ago.” He was sympathetic to artists’ plight, but seemed unsurprised by the company’s indifference. “They should have allowed artists to have recourse in this and a warning to debate,” he said, “but I’ve been told by former employees they see customer service as a waste of profits since they have such a high market share and remain ubiquitous.”
Much of the frustration from artists stems from the lack of communication and recourse. Nerdcore rapper Insane Ian posted that he “had an original song taken down with no warning, and they wouldn’t tell me why either.” Rapper King Chase also struggled to get through to a person at DistroKid. He told The Verge that an entire album for an artist he had been working with was removed with no communication or explanation. “The album had been up for 3-4 years without incident,” he said, and that there had been “no copyright strikes or anything either.”
Amanda Ferri, DistroKid’s VP of Artist Services, told The Verge that “A very small number of recordings distributed through DistroKid have been removed in response to claims made by UMG. We strongly dispute the allegations underlying UMG’s lawsuit and regret the disruption to affected artists. We are working to minimize that disruption while protecting artists’ ability to release their music.”
Update October 10th, 2026: Added comment from Jesse Cannon.

title_en: This Android Auto problem is affecting calls on foldable phones
title_fa: This Android Auto problem is affecting calls on foldable phones
excerpt_en: Gemini might be causing some issues with Android Auto.
excerpt_fa: Gemini might be causing some issues with Android Auto.
content_en:
This Android Auto problem is affecting calls on foldable phones
It seems like Gemini is to blame.
Owners of foldable phones are reportedly running into issues when trying to place outgoing calls using Android Auto. Posts on Reddit, as well as Google and Motorola forums, describe various foldable phones losing their ability to make calls when they're closed, as first reported by Android Authority. And Gemini might play a role in the calling quandary.
Users say that when their phones are closed and they instruct them to call someone, the call doesn't connect. One poster on Reddit said they get a message to "flip open to continue." Incoming calls seem to come through just fine. Several of the posters report the issue only started after they began using Gemini.
While there's no confirmation yet on what may be causing the bug, both Google and Motorola appear to be investigating. Responses in forums show company representatives collecting information about the incidents.
Which foldable phones are affected?
So far, most of the posts mention the Motorola Razr Ultra (specifically the 60 and 70 models) with Android 16 installed. A post from April mentioned issues with a Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 7 and also noted that there were no calling issues until the poster started using Gemini. Android 16 started rolling out in June 2025 with updates like live notification updates, camera improvements and scam detection features.
In that same Reddit post from about three months ago, one user said they had to switch back from Gemini to Google Assistant. After doing so, they were once again able to place outgoing calls while the foldable was closed. While that might seem like an easy enough fix, as of last month, Google pulled Google Assistant from phones, tablets and other devices. The transition began September 4, 2026 but only for phones that have the minimum requirements to run the AI service.
Is there a workaround?
Google and Motorola haven't issued any official fixes yet, and although foldable phone owners have detailed the lengths they've gone to in order to solve the problem, there doesn't seem to be a solution yet aside from making calls with the phones open.
The increased presence of Gemini across the Google ecosystem mirrors the broader push to integrate AI tools into everyday life. While some embrace the myriad AI tools popping up at every turn, others are less convinced, particularly in these early days when bugs may run amok. For some, like a few in these forum threads, the answer is turning to apps and products that don't use AI — or at least offer a way to turn it off.

title_en: How to quickly check your Samsung Galaxy's warranty info
title_fa: How to quickly check your Samsung Galaxy's warranty info
excerpt_en: You don't have to guess how long is left on your Samsung device's warranty; the company makes it easy to confirm.
excerpt_fa: You don't have to guess how long is left on your Samsung device's warranty; the company makes it easy to confirm.
content_en:
How to quickly check your Samsung Galaxy's warranty info
Find out if your Galaxy is covered by its warranty or if you should look elsewhere for service.
If something goes wrong with your Samsung Galaxy phone or tablet, you should first check whether it's still under warranty. On newer devices running One UI 9, Samsung made that process easier by adding a dedicated warranty menu to the Settings app. But even if you're on older software, there are still several ways to check your coverage.
Through Settings in One UI 9
If your Galaxy device is running One UI 9, the process is simple: head to Settings > Warranty and care. This menu includes warranty information, diagnostics, repair options and Samsung Care+ coverage and enrollment info.
At the top, you'll find your device's warranty details, including its coverage type and expiration date. If you have other Galaxy devices linked to your Samsung account, you'll find their info there, too.
The menu also includes built-in diagnostics for hardware like the battery, charging system, screen, camera and sensors. If it flags a problem, you can jump to repair options in the same menu. There's even an option to ask Bixby for troubleshooting help, in case a chatbot can actually address your problem.
Use Samsung Members on older devices
If you aren't yet on One UI 9 (or your device is too old to receive it), Samsung Members lets you register your device and access support. The app is usually pre-installed on Galaxy devices, but if it's missing, you can also download it from the Galaxy Store or Google Play Store.
To check your warranty status, open Samsung Members, sign in and tap Support in the bottom menu. (Older versions may show Get help instead.) From there, you can register your device (if it didn't do so automatically during setup), check its status and access support tools. Depending on your device, app version and region, the app might also show product and warranty details. If not, there's one more place to look.
Use Samsung's website for warranty checks
Should all else fail, Samsung's website is the best fallback. Open Samsung's online devices portal and sign in to your Samsung account. If the device is already registered, you can check its warranty status under My Products. If it isn't, you may need to enter its serial number or IMEI during registration. You can find those on your device under Settings > About phone (or About tablet).

title_en: What is ray tracing in gaming and does it really make a difference?
title_fa: What is ray tracing in gaming and does it really make a difference?
excerpt_en: Ray tracing makes light's behavior more realistic in supported games, but your PC has to use a lot of horsepower to make that happen.
excerpt_fa: Ray tracing makes light's behavior more realistic in supported games, but your PC has to use a lot of horsepower to make that happen.
content_en:
What is ray tracing in gaming and does it really make a difference?
Games look way more beautiful, but it comes at a high cost.
One of the main selling points of the current console generation is that Sony and Microsoft's machines can finally handle ray tracing (RT) at a decent level. Yet while the PS5 and Xbox Series X can provide moderate ray-traced experiences, the top end of the PC gaming food chain is on an entirely different level. High-end rigs offer the most advanced RT features with incredible fidelity. But what if you're on an aging or average PC? Is ray tracing really worth enabling?
It all comes down to the hardware you're using. If your GPU is more than five years old, any ray-traced games your PC is capable of running will likely perform poorly. Ray tracing is a luxury gaming feature that should only be turned on if you own a fairly high-end rig. And that's not even mentioning its flashier sibling: path tracing.
Is ray tracing worth it?
For your average PC gamer playing on a middling GPU, ray tracing will cost too many frames to make it worth enabling. That said, at time of writing, the Steam Hardware Survey ranks the extremely capable NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 as the graphics card with the highest usage share. We thus see dedicated PC players are embracing graphics cards more than capable of handling ray tracing. If your GPU is a couple of generations old, though, RT should be disabled.
But what is ray tracing exactly? In short, it's an advanced rendering technique that simulates realistic lighting effects, shadows and reflections more accurately than old-school rasterization methods. In older games that don't support ray tracing, screen-space reflections are used, which aren't very accurate. By contrast, modern titles that support RT can reflect offscreen objects and shadows by bouncing rays around the screen, before accurately calculating how the in-game world should be lit.
I've been enjoying ray tracing in some of the best PC games for years, and I absolutely adore the technology. There are a couple of major caveats, though. I'm fortunate to have access to an RTX 5090, and I often don't mind embracing NVIDIA's DLSS 4.5 Multi Frame Generation tech to boost my frame rates (at the admitted cost of increased input lag).
For folks gaming on an RTX 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600 XT, there's no way I can recommend ray tracing. Instead, focus on locking down a stable frame rate at your monitor's native resolution. After all, if you've never seen ray tracing in action, you're not going to miss it.
How much does ray tracing impact FPS?
"A whole lot," is the succinct answer. Though it depends on the specific game you're booting up, performance in many modern AAA PC titles will often plummet once you enable ray tracing features, unless you're rocking a seriously powerful rig. You can improve your fps for smoother gaming by turning on DLSS or embracing frame generation, sure. Yet if you're not into frame rate-boosting AI tech, ray tracing can be a performance killer.
A while back, TechSpot analyzed the impact of ray tracing across a whopping 36 different games. During the site's comprehensive testing, average FPS dropped between 20 to 40 percent when RT was on. That's a whole lot of frames to sacrifice for a fancy lighting technique many folks will struggle to notice in motion.
Some of the worst offenders, according to the report: Hogwarts Legacy saw a 45 percent dip in frame rates; for Alan Wake 2 the decrease is around 52 percent, and Hitman 3's average frame rate drops by an absurd 65 percent. I've played Agent 47's latest assassination adventure with RT cranked to the max, and as much I admire all of those geometrically correct rays bouncing off the chrome dome killer's head, that's a brutal performance hit.
Ray tracing vs. path tracing: what's the difference?
Permit me to indulge in a nerdy Star Wars analogy: if ray tracing is a talented Padawan, path tracing is a full-blown Jedi Master. Path tracing is still a type of RT, but a more advanced one. In the handful of PC games that deploy this incredibly pretty technique, the results are often jaw-dropping.
Path tracing — sometimes referred to as "full ray tracing" in certain titles — can calculate far more lighting sources than traditional RT. In games that don't support path tracing, RT is often combined with traditional rasterization methods, with ray tracing handling specific effects like reflections or shadows. Path tracing works differently. Compared to standard RT, it usually controls the entire look of a game, leading to a more consistently lit image.
I replayed the opening scene of Resident Evil Requiem for this feature and compared its High ray tracing preset to the full path tracing option (as you can see in the screenshot above). If you're reading this on your phone, you probably won't be able to spot the differences between the two techs. But they definitely exist.
Path tracing's multi-bounce global illumination is most clearly seen in the car's left headlight. Notice the slight red tinge being cast by the neon lights from a nearby, off-screen shop window. This is absent with ray tracing, where bounce lighting is more limited. If you squint, you can also see that path tracing handles the specular reflections on the car's windshield more effectively, exhibiting less aliasing compared to standard RT. Trust me, it's a lot easier to spot the difference when looking at an uncompressed 4K image.
As much as I admire path tracing in the likes of 007: First Light and Cyberpunk 2077, it's even more brutally taxing on frame rates than traditional ray tracing. With the latter title, enabling path tracing can be 50 percent more demanding than RT depending on the scene. Unless you're lucky enough to own an RTX 5090 or RTX 5080, you're best off steering well clear of the gorgeous but performance-punishing tech.

title_en: Anthropic says its AI agents tried to break into government websites
title_fa: Anthropic says its AI agents tried to break into government websites
excerpt_en: In its latest report, Anthropic has revealed that its AI agents meddled with government websites during testing.
excerpt_fa: In its latest report, Anthropic has revealed that its AI agents meddled with government websites during testing.
content_en:
Anthropic says its AI agents tried to break into government websites
The company didn’t name them, but the affected agencies were ‘at the federal, state and local levels.’
Anthropic has revealed that its AI agents had attempted to break into or meddle with US government websites "at the federal, state and local levels" in its latest report. The company didn't name specific agencies and organizations in the report to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems at their request. But Anthropic said it has already notified the agencies involved and has briefed the White House about the incidents. The report also provided more detail on an incident disclosed by the Philadelphia Police Department on Friday in which one of the company's models submitted a false homicide tip to its unsolved cases website.
That instance involved Claude Haiku 4.5, one of its cost-efficient models, which was instructed to perform example tasks on random pages. It found a page referencing an unsolved homicide case with a tip form. As you may have guessed, Claude filled out the form and submitted a tip. It said: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to The New York Times that Anthropic recently notified its office about the submission. It said the tip was dated July 18 and that it was flagged as spam, so the department at least didn't waste resources investigating it.
In another instance, Anthropic made Claude Mythos 5, its cybersecurity-focused model, identify a location shown in a photo. Claude tried to access a government property map to triangulate its guesses, because it could not click links on web pages like a person could. It found access tokens instead and sent inquiry requests straight to the map's server to gain access to its data. Mythos 5 also requested an access token from a state agency website to pull data for a statistics task without paying a fee that visitors were supposed to pay.
Anthropic discovered these events upon reviewing transcripts of its evaluations. It started looking through them in July, after OpenAI had admitted that its agents escaped their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face without prompting. OpenAI also confirmed in September that its agents had meddled with government websites, particularly those operated by the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
In the Remediation section of its report, Anthropic said it has "taken several preventative measures" after discovering the unintended model actions. "Some of the public evaluations we no longer run; others we have moved to their offline versions, or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites," the report states. "We've also made broader changes. We have updated the guardrails on some of our internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them." Anthropic also says it's "built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described" in the report, among other measures.

title_en: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
title_fa: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
excerpt_en: The startup says its fuel cells are super efficient and cut fuel costs during a time when the tech industry can’t get enough electricity.
excerpt_fa: The startup says its fuel cells are super efficient and cut fuel costs during a time when the tech industry can’t get enough electricity.
content_en:
As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power.
Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles.
Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight.
The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.”
Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.”
As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said.
Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department.
Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said.
“Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.”
The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said.
Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said.
Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. You can catch all the action this coming week in downtown San Francisco at Moscone West.

title_en: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
title_fa: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
excerpt_en: Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger...
excerpt_fa: Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger...
content_en:
Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger has confirmed that “one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.”
Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.
A spy implant in some Ledger crypto wallets may be the root of an $86 million supply chain attack.
Photos and videos posted on X and Threads appear to show a small circuit board sandwiched under the screen. The implant allegedly intercepts anything displayed on the screen, including the seed passphrase shown during the initial setup. Using an embedded SIM card, the implant then sends that information back to the attacker, who can then siphon funds from user accounts.
Reports indicate that whoever is behind the hack has stolen over $86 million worth of crypto from hundreds of wallets. There’s no indication that Ledger’s systems have been compromised or that wallets purchased directly from the company have been affected. Instead, the issue appears to be a supply chain attack primarily involving users in Southeast Asia and the CryptoBillis reseller. Ledger has provided guidance on how to check if your wallet has been tampered with.
Update October 10th, 2026: Added additional statment from Ledger.

title_en: How to reset your Samsung TV
title_fa: How to reset your Samsung TV
excerpt_en: If you have a Frame TV or one of the other Samsung models, you may occasionally need to reboot or factory reset it.
excerpt_fa: If you have a Frame TV or one of the other Samsung models, you may occasionally need to reboot or factory reset it.
content_en:
How to reset your Samsung TV
If your Frame or other Samsung TV is acting up, give these resets a try,
Resetting devices is, oddly enough, an essential skill in the modern tech landscape. Aside from the fact that selling or trading devices like smartphones and laptops is incredibly common, it's an effective troubleshooting technique. Factory resets force a device to revert to its out-of-the-box state, including options, processes and installed apps. It can be a royal pain to get things back the way you like — but it's better than dealing with crashes or broken features.
There are few reasons to reset a smart TV, including Samsung models, yet things do sometimes go haywire. A favorite streaming app might repeatedly freeze no matter how many times you reinstall it, or the OS might develop problems like video glitches. There's no guarantee that a reset will come to the rescue, but it's a good troubleshooting step.
There's not much to performing one on a Samsung TV. Just be sure to try simpler tactics first, some of which we'll go over later. Remember, once you've triggered a factory reset, there's no going back. On top of reconfiguring picture and sound preferences, you'll be redownloading apps and OS updates.
All you need to know about factory resetting your Samsung TV
Before initiating a factory reset, be sure you have any PIN codes and passwords written down somewhere, including the logins for streaming apps and your Wi-Fi router. Once the reset is complete, you'll need these to get back to watching anything. Unless, perhaps, you're content with over-the-air TV, Blu-ray or a connected game console or PC. Even then, you may want to get back online briefly to install updates for Tizen, Samsung's OS.
Once you're sure you want to go ahead, follow these steps:
1. From the home screen, select Settings.
2. Click All Settings.

title_en: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
title_fa: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
excerpt_en: Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform.
excerpt_fa: Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform.
content_en:
Cloudflare announced Friday that it’s acquiring Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name.
According to Cloudflare’s Kenton Varda, Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform, which allows customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network. (Varda is principal engineer for Cloudflare Workers.)
Deno — which was co-founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl — recently launched celld, an open source implementation of Workers, which Varda wrote “delighted” the Cloudflare team. Varda argued that contrary to “a popular theory” that the company “made Cloudflare Workers work differently from other cloud platforms in order to create ‘lock-in,’” the company believes “being open source and giving people an escape hatch is good business.”
Dahl, meanwhile, wrote that his team is “joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model a mainstream way to build servers.”
The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Deno had raised a total of $26 million, including a Series A led by Sequoia.

title_en: GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
title_fa: GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
excerpt_en: A shortage has driven resale prices through the roof.
excerpt_fa: A shortage has driven resale prices through the roof.
content_en:
GameStop is hoping PS5 Pro buyers are desperate enough to pay $500 over MSRP
A used PS5 Pro will run you about $1,400.
As the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches, gamers are scrambling to maximize gameplay with the most advanced consoles on the market. Advertised as PS5 Pro Enhanced, the game comes as Sony faces a shortage of its popular console. With the AI boom consuming the world's silicon, Sony has struggled to maintain its production cycles, leading to a global shortage of the console that is likely to last well into 2027.
Released in 2024, Sony now prices its advanced console $200 higher than its initial asking price, listing it at a whopping $899.99. However, you may end up paying well above this already inflated price tag if you are looking to snag a new console by the end of the year. As it stands, retailers and resellers alike are taking the laws of supply and demand to heart. GameStop, for instance, currently lists a used PlayStation 5 Pro for an eye-popping $1,399.99, half a grand over its MSRP. Similar markups can be found across the resale market.
Sony has attempted to dampen these markups where it can. In Japan, for instance, the company instituted a lottery system tied to game time minimums, presumably to rein in a reseller market that is quickly getting out of control. However, with no end to the shortage in sight, inflated prices are only likely to persist.
A runaway market
The PS5 Pro is indicative of broader trends in the consumer tech market. Data centers are gobbling up high-bandwidth memory, a key component for delivering data quickly to advanced processors. The cascading effect has seen the production of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) necessary for consumer devices like the PS5 Pro lag, sparking shortages. An August 2026 JP Morgan report predicted that by the end of the year, the price of DRAM will have risen 400 percent worldwide since the PS5 Pro was released in 2024.
These trends are likely to persist. In September 2026, German gaming publication Playfront reported that internal memos between Sony and its distribution partners state that the PS5 Pro shortage would persist "through early 2027 at the earliest." Some expect the component constraints to persist far beyond next year, with some forecasting that the RAM crisis could persist until the 2030.
GameStop is just one of several sellers attempting to squeeze every last drop out of the PlayStation 5 Pro shortage. Best Buy, for instance, is currently selling the console for over $1,500. Walmart, meanwhile, is selling an open box version of the console for $1,200. These prices are largely in line with the resale market, with prices on eBay regularly soaring above $1,100. For what its worth, GameStop owns roughly 10 percent of the online marketplace, and attempted a $56 billion unsolicited takeover of the company earlier this year.
The exorbitant prices sparked by Sony's PlayStation 5 Pro crisis are quickly becoming the norm for most consumer tech products. According to a September 2026 report by The Economist, the consumer price index for "computer software and accessories" skyrocketed by 31 percent. In addition to the PS5 Pro's $200 increase, PlayStation 5s have increased by $150, roughly 30 percent. Such trends could prove catastrophic for the industry. This month, video game hardware sales hit a 13-year low.
Is it worth the pricetag?
Before splurging on GameStop's PS5 Pro, you may want to ask whether the upgrade is worth the cash. Capable of running 4K graphics at 60 frames per second, the PS5 Pro's enhanced visuals look great on a high-end television. Add 2 TB of memory, an enhanced GPU and special features like ray tracing, andthe PS5 Pro delivers tangible advantages over its predecessor.
The greatest advancement is its PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) image upscaler, which uses AI to enhance image pixels. Although somewhat maligned at its initial release, PlayStation made an improved edition, PSSR Enhanced, that is now the console's default setting. However, like many of the Pro's most compelling features, PSSR only works for games labeled PS5 Pro Enhanced, like GTA VI. To date, however, you and a friend could probably count the number of games that natively use the new PSSR on your hands. Whether these visual upgrades meaningfully change the gaming experience, though, is debated.
Sony's latest PS5 update may begin to narrow the gap between the two consoles. In an October 2026 blog post, Sony stated that it was bringing a similar AI upscaling functionality known as Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) to the PS5. Although not described by Sony as the "gold standard" of PSSR, QSSR will bring image and stability improvements to the PS5.
Overall, the PlayStation 5 Pro is a more powerful, visually compelling console to its predecessor. However, many reviewers already questioned whether these enhancements were worth the PS5 Pro's initial price tag. Given that GameStop is selling the advanced console for nearly double the 2024 asking price, and $500 above MSRP, its safe to say that breaking the bank for the PS5 Pro likely isn't worth it.
